credit: NASA, via the NSSDCA master catalog

caption: Full disk view of Mars photographed by Mariner 7 on approach in 1969 from about 200,000 miles, showing the polar caps and the ring shaped feature then catalogued as Nix Olympica, which Mariner 9 later identified as the volcano Olympus Mons.
credit: NASA, via NASA on The Commons

caption: Colour view of Mars assembled by combining three Mariner 7 black and white frames taken through different colour filters. The cameras themselves were monochrome.
credit: NASA, reproduced in NASA technical report NTRS 19730005151

caption: Wide-angle Mariner 6 and Mariner 7 frames laid onto a globe already carrying an indistinct Earth-based view of Mars. The Mariner 6 pictures form the two upper rows; the Mariner 7 pictures run from centre to lower right and across the south polar cap.
credit: NASA, via NASA on The Commons

caption: A colour photograph of an M-69 spacecraft standing in a high bay assembly hall with technicians in white coats around it and on a work platform beside it, showing the large spherical propellant tank, the plumbing loop across the body, a solar panel and the parabolic high gain antenna. Wikimedia records the subject as the verification of systems unit for Mars 1969A.
credit: Soviet factory photograph, photographer unrecorded; published by NASA/NSSDCA and mirrored on Wikimedia Commons

caption: A Soviet design drawing of the АМС «M-69» in two views, with Russian callouts naming the solar panels, the descent vehicle (спускаемый аппарат), the fuel tank, the engine, the parabolic high gain antenna, the instrument compartment, the radiator heater, the omnidirectional antenna, the astro navigation system and the attitude control nozzles. The same drawing is Figure 5 of V. G. Perminov's NASA monograph, captioned there 'The M-69 Spacecraft (Second Version)', where the key is translated into English and item (2) is given as 'lander'.
credit: НПО Лавочкина (NPO Lavochkin), via RussianSpaceWeb.com (Anatoly Zak)

caption: A small vertical photograph of an M-69 spacecraft part way through assembly, wrapped in protective covers, with the two camera window shrouds and the plumbing loop visible. RussianSpaceWeb captions it 'The Mars M-69 spacecraft during the assembly' and credits NPO Lavochkin.
credit: НПО Лавочкина (NPO Lavochkin), via RussianSpaceWeb.com (Anatoly Zak)

caption: A colour studio photograph of a surviving PrOP-M laid on a white surface, showing the flat black body, the wide flat ski down each side, the aluminium penetrometer turret bolted to the top deck and the pair of thin obstacle rods projecting from the far end; Komsomolskaya Pravda's caption reads that the world's first Mars rover was only the size of a large book, and its article states that three Leningrad-built units survive, one at NPO Lavochkin, one at VNIITransMash and one on show in the Museum of Cosmonautics in the Peter and Paul Fortress, without tying this studio frame to any one of them.
credit: Артем КИЛЬКИН (Artyom Kilkin) / Фотобанк КП, Комсомольская правда

caption: The PrOP-M photographed from above and to one side on a red-brown surface, with both skis, the black instrument box, the penetrometer turret and the link rods that threw the skis forward all visible; this is the frame Russian sources reproduce for the machine itself, credited to the institute that built it.
credit: ВНИИТрансмаш; published in Куприянов В., Иванян Г., Новости космонавтики, 2001, № 12

caption: A man in a dark jacket holds a PrOP-M in both hands in a museum gallery, standing beside a plinth carrying a pair of Lunokhod chassis wheels with their white hub drive units and a bilingual label, under a large wall picture of a Lunokhod on a grey landscape. That wall picture is a ground publicity shot of the rover posed on a simulated lunar surface. Nothing on the Moon could have photographed Lunokhod 1 from outside.
credit: Артем КИЛЬКИН (Artyom Kilkin) / Фотобанк КП, Комсомольская правда

caption: A full-size replica of the Mars 3 lander on a stand in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, the four petal covers folded back on their springs, antennas and instrument booms extended, and a flat black box with side rails and two thin rods sitting on top of the sphere in the position PrOP-M occupied.
credit: Музей Космонавтики (Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics, Moscow), via Flickr and Wikimedia Commons, CC0

caption: A 230 dram Armenian stamp of 2021 carrying the designer's name in Armenian script and ALEXANDER KEMURDZHIAN in Latin, ARMENIA up the left edge and the dates 1921-2003, with a photographic portrait of the designer in heavy glasses at the right, a colour illustration of a Lunokhod on a brown surface at the left and engineering drawings behind them.
credit: HayPost (Armenian postal operator), scan via Colnect and Wikimedia Commons

caption: A grayscale Context Camera mosaic view of a large, shallow, heavily degraded Martian crater with the place label Kemurdzhian printed across its floor by the mapping software used to take the screenshot; the IAU gazetteer gives the crater a diameter of 61 km, centred near 43.2 degrees south and 188.6 degrees east, with the name approved on 15 September 2020.
credit: NASA/JPL/MSSS/The Murray Lab, CTX global mosaic, via Wikimedia Commons

caption: A large labelled drawing of the M-71C spacecraft with Russian callouts and a thirteen item English key, naming the astro navigation optics, the instrument module, the magnetometer, the stereo antenna, the high gain parabolic antenna, the low gain cone antennas, the propulsion tanks, the thermal radiators, the attitude and stabilisation nozzles and the solar panels. Perminov captions this figure as the M-71C, the vehicle the Soviets flew as Kosmos 419; NSSDCA hosts the same scan under a Mars 2 and Mars 3 filename because the orbiters were built on the same bus.
credit: NASA/NSSDCA, from V. G. Perminov, The Difficult Road to Mars, NASA Monographs in Aerospace History No. 15, 1999

caption: A small black and white photograph of a Soviet planetary spacecraft with a large parabolic high gain antenna, solar panels and an instrument compartment, standing on a stand in a factory hall. The URL was fetched and returns a valid JPEG, but the provenance and rights could not be established, so it is flagged unverified.
credit: Source not established. Uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by user B2322858; the original photographer and rights holder could not be traced.

caption: Technicians installing solar panels on the spacecraft then known by its pre-launch letter as Mariner H, in a clean room at Cape Kennedy in 1971. NASA's caption notes it would be designated Mariner 8 following launch.
credit: NASA / John F. Kennedy Space Center, photo KSC-71PC-0343

caption: The Mariner Mars 1971 spacecraft photographed in flight configuration against black, with the thermal blanketed propulsion module on top and the science scan platform beneath. Mariner 8 and Mariner 9 were built to the same design; NASA uses this portrait as the lead image of its Mariner 8 mission page, and it is the same photograph this catalogue also shows under Mariner 9.

NASA labelled diagram of the Mariner Mars 1971 spacecraft in two views, marking the maneuver engine and propulsion tanks, the four solar panels, and the scan platform instruments: wide-angle TV, narrow-angle TV, ultraviolet spectrometer, infrared radiometer and infrared interferometer spectrometer. NASA captions it as the Mariner 1971 series and runs it on its Mariner 8 page; Mariner 8 and Mariner 9 were identical.
A technician checking the spacecraft, still known by its pre-launch letter as Mariner I, before encapsulation for launch. The NASA caption records the launch as 6:23 p.m. EDT on 30 May 1971.
credit: NASA / John F. Kennedy Space Center, photo KSC-71P-0366

caption: Mariner 9 approach picture taken at 8:46 a.m. PST on 11 November 1971 from about 408,000 miles, one of 31 frames on the first tape load. The dust storm has wiped the surface featureless; the dark spot near the top was tentatively identified as Nix Olympica, and NASA's caption already suggested it might be a high mountain showing through the dust.
credit: NASA/JPL, via NASA on The Commons

caption: Mosaic of Mariner 9 frames from the first orbit showing the remnants of the south polar cap dimly through the dust storm, paired with the same region as Mariner 7 photographed it in August 1969.
credit: NASA, via NASA on The Commons

caption: Mosaic of Mariner 9 frames from revolutions 146 and 148 on 8 March 1972, the first clear view of Olympus Mons after the dust settled, showing the summit caldera complex and the basal scarp that rings the volcano.
credit: NASA/JPL; mosaic by Justin Cowart, CC BY 2.0

caption: Mariner 9 mosaic taken on 5 January 1972 during revolution 106, running from Valles Marineris south across Solis Planum to the rim of the Argyre basin. This is genuine Mariner 9 data, unlike the famous full length Valles Marineris mosaic that usually illustrates the canyon, which is Viking.
credit: NASA/JPL; mosaic by Justin Cowart, CC BY 2.0

caption: Phobos photographed from 5,760 km on orbit 89, frame MTVS 4109-9. NSSDCA notes that craters as small as 300 m are visible and that the moon is about 26 km along its longest axis.
credit: NASA, via the NSSDCA photo gallery

caption: NASA studio photograph of the Mariner Mars 1971 spacecraft in flight configuration against black: the thermal blanketed propulsion module on top, four solar panels spanning 6.89 m, and the science scan platform slung underneath. Mariner 8 and Mariner 9 were built to the same design, the Commons file carries the Mariner H mission text, and NASA publishes this same photograph as the lead image of its Mariner 8 page, so it cannot be tied to one airframe.

A factory photograph of an M-71 interplanetary station of the type flown as Mars 2 and Mars 3, standing on its trolley in the assembly hall with the high-gain dish and both solar wings deployed and a technician working at the left wing.
A HiRISE image acquired by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter specifically to search for the Mars 2 debris field, released by JPL in October 2014 under the title Search for the Mars 2 Debris Field.

A Soviet cutaway illustration of the M-71 descent module titled спускаемый аппарат, labelled in Russian for the drogue-deploy motor, the parachute container, the main parachute, the radio altimeter antenna, the aerodynamic brake cone and the automatic Mars station inside.
A modern computer rendering of the PrOP-M walking rover, the 4.5 kg tethered robot carried by both Mars 2 and Mars 3, showing the two skis and the instrument box.
credit: Joris Wegner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

caption: A 6 kopeck Soviet stamp reading Автоматическая станция «Марс-2»: вымпел на планете 27.11.71 г., with an artist's painting of the station firing its engine near Mars and an inset of the pennant carrying the Soviet coat of arms.
credit: Почта СССР (USSR Post); scan by Andrew Butko, via Wikimedia Commons

caption: A 1971 archival photograph captioned АМС «Марс-3», showing the assembled station from above with the high-gain dish, both solar wings, the low-gain antenna boom and the descent module in its brake shield at the top.
credit: РГАНТД (Russian State Archive of Scientific and Technical Documentation), Арх. № 1-2409

caption: A ground photograph of the automatic Mars station in its landed configuration, the four petals folded back, the antennas and instrument booms extended and the two panoramic telephotometer heads visible at the top of the sphere.

A Soviet descent module during ground testing, sitting inside its conical aerodynamic brake shield with the parachute container and the sealed station above it. NPO Lavochkin publishes this frame on its Mars 2 and Mars 3 page, while NASA's NSSDCA catalogue publishes the same frame as the M-73P descent module of the 1973 missions, so which article it shows is not settled.

The print made from the 79 lines of phototelevision signal Mars 3 sent from the surface on 2 December 1971. It is a grey band with a light margin and no horizon; Soviet analysts reported that it contains no information, and later readings of what it holds still disagree.
credit: USSR, Mars 3 lander telephotometer, via Wikimedia Commons (scan sourced from The Planetary Society)

caption: A 1971 photograph of the real PrOP-M rover built by Alexander Kemurdzhian's team at VNIITransMash, the small tethered box on two walking skis that Mars 3 carried to the surface.
credit: ВНИИТрансмаш; published in Куприянов В., Иванян Г., Новости космонавтики, 2001, № 12

caption: The 2013 HiRISE release Could This Be the Mars Soviet 3 Lander, four panels showing features on the floor of Ptolemaeus crater identified by Russian enthusiasts as the possible parachute, heat shield, terminal retrorocket and lander of Mars 3.
A Mars 3 orbiter phototelevision frame of the Martian limb taken from roughly 150,000 km during the 1971 global dust storm, processed by Don P. Mitchell from published Soviet source material.
credit: Don P. Mitchell (image processing), mentallandscape.com; original data USSR

caption: A factory photograph of an M-73 station in the assembly hall at the Lavochkin plant, solar wings and high-gain dish deployed, with the conical shroud of the upper section above the toroidal instrument compartment.

An archive print of a Martian surface photograph returned by the 1973 M-73 expedition, showing cratered terrain with the camera's reseau cross marks across the frame and a grey scale calibration wedge along the bottom edge. The Lavochkin page gives no frame number or date.

A colour composite of Mars assembled from Mars 5 frames 3, 4 and 5 of imaging programme 5 on 26 February 1974, taken through the green, red and blue filters of the 52 mm Vega camera and combined by Don P. Mitchell.
credit: Don P. Mitchell (image processing), mentallandscape.com; original data USSR

caption: Mars 5 frame 4.Z from imaging programme 1 on 17 February 1974, taken with the 350 mm Zulfar telephoto camera through its orange filter and processed by Don P. Mitchell.
credit: Don P. Mitchell (image processing), mentallandscape.com; original data USSR

caption: A Soviet Mars descent module during ground testing on Earth, captioned on Russian Wikipedia as the M-73P descent module, the type carried by Mars 6 and Mars 7, sitting in its conical aerodynamic brake shield.
credit: NASA NSSDCA catalogue (entry 1973-053A); underlying photograph USSR, NPO Lavochkin

caption: A Soviet numbered technical illustration of the M-73 orbiter, an external view rather than a sectioned cutaway, keyed 2 to 7 for the high-gain dish, the upper instrument assembly, the radiators, the solar wings and the propellant tank section.

A Soviet presentation sheet headed АВТОМАТИЧЕСКИЙ КОСМИЧЕСКИЙ КОМПЛЕКС-5М, showing the vehicle with its umbrella shield opened, the mass written as ВЕС КОСМИЧЕСКОГО АППАРАТА 8700 +75 КГ, five numbered callouts reading descent vehicle, return vehicle, ascent rocket, landing platform and trajectory block, and two small scale views at the right, the plan one dimensioned about 11.7 m across.
credit: RussianSpaceWeb.com (Anatoly Zak); underlying sheet Soviet, no separate credit given on the page

caption: A modern 3D cutaway rendering of the two Proton-K launches that would have assembled one 5M mission, the left rocket carrying the 11S86 active space tug with its docking port, rendezvous antennas and avionics, the right carrying the 11S824M passive tug with the 5M sample return spacecraft above it and its deployable Mars entry shield, labelled TZU, folded inside the payload fairing.

An unflown Viking lander biology instrument on museum display, opened so that two of the three experiment modules are visible with their original engineering labels reading MODULE ASSEMBLY PYROLYSIS EXPERIMENT and MODULE ASSEMBLY LABELED RELEASE EXPERIMENT. The photographer records the object as being on display at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

A close-up inside a Viking Lander Biology Instrument, a ground unit that never flew, photographed by Steve Jurvetson in the Future Ventures space collection. Valve blocks, tubing, potting compound and wiring of the three life detection experiments are visible. The flight instruments packed the pyrolytic release, labeled release and gas exchange experiments into about 28 litres, roughly one cubic foot, for a mass of 15.5 kg.

A NASA cutaway line drawing of the Viking lander biology instrument, calling out the pyrolytic release, labeled release and gas exchange experiments, the carbon-14 detector assembly, the carrousel, the nutrient reservoir, the soil distribution assembly and the gas chromatograph.

A Viking gas chromatograph mass spectrometer in the National Air and Space Museum collection, opened and labelled to show the mass spectrometer, the gas chromatograph column, the effluent splitter and separator, the soil loader and soil ovens and the hydrogen carrier gas tank. The museum records this unit as identical to the instruments carried to Mars, so it is a ground twin rather than a flown spacecraft part. Built by Litton Systems and transferred to the museum by NASA and JPL.
credit: National Air and Space Museum, Smithsonian Institution (artifact A19800074000)

caption: A trench dug in Chryse Planitia by the Viking 1 surface sampler collector head, cut by extending the head from lower right toward upper left and then withdrawing it, with lumpy piles of excavated material at the end of the trench.

A technician in a clean-room smock handling the Viking lander's extendable surface sampler boom and collector head in a 1971 NASA photograph, with a Viking lander standing on its three legs behind him.

Viking flight controllers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, with the display board reading 13 JUL 76 UTC and the spacecraft status board listing Viking 1, Viking 2, Helios 1, Helios 2, Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 alongside their launch, encounter and landing dates.
credit: John Malmin / Los Angeles Times, UCLA Library Digital Collections

caption: The first photograph ever taken from the surface of Mars, scanned by Viking 1 camera 2 starting about 25 seconds after touchdown on 20 July 1976, showing rocks, fine soil and one of the lander's footpads at lower right.

The Viking lander proof test article, genuine Viking ground-test hardware rather than a flown spacecraft, photographed in the Milestones of Flight gallery at the National Air and Space Museum on 24 June 2016. The high-gain antenna dish, the sampler arm boom at right and the two footpads are all visible.
credit: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, photo by Mark Avino (NASM2016-02690)

caption: Viking 1 leaves Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral on a Titan IIIE-Centaur at 5:22 p.m. EDT on 20 August 1975, which is 21:22 UT, on the third launch attempt after two scrubs.

The first colour picture from the surface of Mars, taken by Viking 1 on 21 July 1976, the day after landing, looking southeast across Chryse Planitia at about local noon, with orange-red surface material, scattered rocks and a reddish sky.

The Viking 1 lander picked out from Mars orbit by the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in observation PSP_001521_2025, the image that fixed the lander's measured position in western Chryse Planitia.

A section of Viking Orbiter 1 frame 035A72, taken on 25 July 1976 while the orbiter was scouting Viking 2 landing sites in the Cydonia region at about 47 metres per pixel. The black specks scattered across the frame are data dropouts in the raw transmission; the ground itself carries no such markings.

The same Cydonia mesa re-photographed in 2001 by the Mars Orbiter Camera on Mars Global Surveyor, at far higher resolution and a different sun angle, resolving it as an eroded landform with layered slopes and a debris apron.

Frost banked around rocks and lying in patches across the soil at the Viking 2 site in Utopia Planitia, photographed on 18 May 1979 and relayed to Earth by Viking Orbiter 1 on 7 June 1979. NASA described it as a thin coating of water ice on the rocks and soil.
credit: NASA (Great Images in NASA, GPN-2000-001706; Viking Lander 2, P-21841)

caption: The blue-filter frame Viking 2 camera 2 took looking due north at 12:59 p.m. local lander time on 13 September 1977, which JPL described as the first clear indication of frost accumulating on the martian surface seen by lander cameras. Frost shows white around the bases of rocks and in a trench dug by the sampler arm, and the lander's own shadow falls across the foreground.
The 18 May 1979 frost scene at the Viking 2 site in colour, released by JPL as PIA00571. NASA's caption notes the frost remained on the surface for about 100 days.

A self-portrait assembled from Viking 2 lander camera frames at Utopia Planitia, showing the circular high-gain antenna, the camera calibration charts and red dust settled on the spacecraft, with a boulder field running to the horizon.
The Viking 2 lander seen from Mars orbit by the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in observation PSP_001501_2280, taken on 21 November 2006.

The assembled spacecraft of the 1F class standing in the high bay at the Lavochkin plant, the two solar wings spread above the instrument section, antennas and instrument booms fitted, the propulsion section and its spherical tanks below, and a man standing at the lower left for scale. Lavochkin publishes the frame in the gallery of its Mars-96 page with no caption and no date.

A penetrator on a trestle in a workshop: a slender white fore-body with instrument ports along it, clamped into a wide conical brake shield, with handling straps under it and factory floor behind. The Lavochkin gallery gives the frame no caption and no date.

A small autonomous surface station lying on a sandy test bed with its four petals folded back around the white central body, springs and hinges visible at each petal root and a wire loop antenna beside it. This is a ground article on Earth, photographed on simulated terrain. Nothing in the frame came from Mars.

A six-wheeled rover chassis of the Marsokhod type, three axles of barrel wheels with a camera mast above it, climbing a pile of dark boulders in Death Valley while a crowd of Planetary Society members and engineers watches from behind and their vehicles stand parked on the flat. The Society's timeline entry for 1992 reads: Society sponsors Mars rover tests in California's Death Valley.

The Marsokhod rover, a Russian six-wheeled chassis carrying American avionics in a red box, a camera mast and an instrument arm, standing on broken lava at Kilauea in Hawaii on 13 February 1995. NASA's catalogue text for the frame reads: Marsokhod Russian Rover explores Kilauea, Hawaii via telepresence for Jason IV Island Earth Projects (Volcano simulates Martian Terrain).
credit: NASA Ames Research Center; photograph by Ed Schilling

caption: A Marsokhod prototype on an exhibition stand at the MAKS-2009 air show near Moscow, its six barrel wheels set into a bed of sand and rock, with a dish antenna, solar panels, coloured cabling and an instrument arm fitted. RussianSpaceWeb captions it as a prototype of the rover which was considered for the M1 mission.
credit: Anatoly Zak, RussianSpaceWeb.com (watermark on the frame); the page caption credits NPO Lavochkin

caption: The Mars balloon in flight during the 1990 desert tests: the long envelope high against a blue sky and broken cloud, the small gondola hanging below it, and the line running down to the desert floor where the guiderope has drawn a track across a dune. The Society's timeline entry for 1990 reads: Planetary Society members support desert testing of the Mars Balloon, slated to fly on the Soviet Mars '96 mission.
credit: The Planetary Society (the page names no photographer; the cover photograph of the same test campaign is credited in the magazine to Charlene M. Anderson)

caption: The cover of The Planetary Report volume XI number 1, January and February 1991, headlined The Mars Balloon: It Works!, carrying a photograph of the balloon aloft over the Mojave with its guiderope trailing to the ground. The cover note inside reads that the French-built Mars Balloon, equipped with the SNAKE guide-rope designed by The Planetary Society, is an intrinsic and official part of the Soviet Mars '94 mission, that during tests in California's Mojave Desert we proved that our design works, and that the photograph is by Charlene M. Anderson.
credit: The Planetary Society; cover photograph by Charlene M. Anderson

caption: A CNES sequence drawing headed AEROSTAT LAUNCHING, tracking the balloon from aerodynamic braking and parachute descent through parachute and balloon separation, deployment and balloon filling, first landing and balloon mission starting, with the rover's separate trajectory dotted across the same panel. The balloon is drawn in two parts, a pale upper cell over a dark lower one, and the guiderope reaches the ground at every stage after the first landing. Drew Ex Machina's caption reads: An early concept from 1988 for the deployment of the French balloon for the Mars 1994 mission. Since then, the rover has been replaced with penetrators.
credit: CNES, as credited by Drew Ex Machina; the drawing is signed david ducros

caption: A CNES painting of the balloon's daily cycle on Mars, the same envelope drawn several times across one panel: high in daylight at the left and right, sinking as the light fails, and resting at night in the middle of the picture with its guiderope lying on the ground under a black sky. Drew Ex Machina's caption reads: Depiction of the daily cycle of the French-made balloon for the Mars 1994 mission.
credit: CNES / David Ducros, as credited by Drew Ex Machina

caption: Mars Global Surveyor standing in a clean room before its 1996 launch, gold thermal blankets over the bus, technicians working at it, and a white arrow with the words Mars Relay pointing at the pale cylindrical mast on the top deck. The MSSS page describes that mast as a quadrifilar helix fibreglass antenna approximately 80 cm tall and 10 cm in diameter.
credit: NASA/JPL and KSC (the image credit printed on the page); Mars Relay label added by Malin Space Science Systems, ©1999 MSSS

mission_name: The sample returns cancelled before this one
caption: A NASA artist's painting, catalogued S87-35313 and dated 15 May 1987, of the Mars Sample Return mission then under joint study by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and the Johnson Space Center. In the foreground a rover built as three linked two-wheeled cabs, carrying a stereo camera vision system and tool-equipped sampling arms, works among boulders; the lander with its ascent rocket stands on the plain in the middle distance and the orbiter crosses the black sky at upper right. NASA's own caption describes a rover that would spend a year collecting rock and soil, drive back to the lander and hand its samples to a small rocket for rendezvous in Mars orbit.

mission_name: The sample returns cancelled before this one
caption: A photograph of Robby, JPL's six-wheeled Mars rover testbed, tilted on a slope during field testing in the arroyo below the laboratory around 1990. The vehicle has three pairs of large knobbly tyres, a body clad in wrinkled gold thermal foil, a stereo camera bar on a mast, a jointed arm reaching down at the left and a white rear body section marked NASA JPL riding on the rearmost pair of wheels. The JPL Robotics gallery caption records that Robby demonstrated six-wheeled autonomous traverses of natural terrain using stereo vision and onboard navigation and carried a PUMA arm for sample gathering; a 1993 JPL survey of rover technology records that JPL built the Robby testbed in 1988 from its Surveyor Lunar Rover Vehicle experience and the mission requirements of the Mars Rover/Sample Return programme.

A colour factory photograph of a 1F Phobos station standing in the assembly hall at the Lavochkin plant, the thermally blanketed spherical propellant tanks of the Autonomous Propulsion Unit filling the lower half, smaller spherical tanks and instrument boxes above them, red protective covers and tags still fitted, a dark solar wing at the right edge and two technicians on a work platform at the left. The Lavochkin gallery carries no caption, date or serial number for the frame.

A Proton-K lying horizontally on its rail transporter at Baikonur, ФОБОС painted in Cyrillic along the payload shroud and ПРОТОН along the core stage, lightning masts and pad structures behind it. Advertising boards for Soviet foreign-trade organisations are fixed along the transporter, among them Avtoexport, VO Stroidormashexport of Moscow and Электроника. The Lavochkin gallery gives the frame no caption or date.

A Soviet artist's painting of the close-approach phase, with the 1F station shown in a sequence of positions along a yellow track, thrusters firing, beams reaching down to the surface of Phobos, and green arrows leading to two deployed payloads: the DAS long-lived autonomous station sitting on the ground with its solar panels unfolded, and a line of small spheres bouncing across the regolith, which is the PrOP-FP hopping probe. Mars fills the upper right. None of it happened.

Four panels of one Phobos observation by the VSK video-spectrometric complex on 25 March 1989, the last of the three imaging passes Phobos 2 completed and returned. Three panels are the raw channel data processed by Don P. Mitchell (wide angle blue-green, narrow angle clear, wide angle near-infrared) and the fourth is the same observation as processed at the Space Research Institute in Moscow, still carrying its Soviet header (С) ИКИ АН СССР ФОБОС 25:03:89. The short white bar low in the near-infrared panel is a known fault in columns 228 to 231 of that CCD, which Mitchell records was later misidentified by UFO writers as an alien spacecraft.
credit: Don P. Mitchell (image processing), mentallandscape.com; original data ИКИ АН СССР (Space Research Institute), via NSSDC

caption: Phobos, about 25 km across, as a dark grey body against the bright orange dust of Mars, from the VSK camera of Phobos 2 on 25 March 1989. The Planetary Society publishes it as a colour composite assembled by Ted Stryk from raw data supplied by the Russian Academy of Sciences, and its caption records that Phobos 2 returned 13 colour sets of Phobos images before contact was lost on 27 March 1989.
credit: Russian Academy of Sciences / Ted Stryk, via The Planetary Society (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0)

caption: One of the four Termoskan panoramas, the thermal infrared channel of the third observing session, which Mitchell labels 26 March 1989 daytime and which matches the archive stop time of 1989-03-26T17:49:50 in NASA's PDS description of the dataset. The long narrow strip runs across the Martian equatorial region at about 1.8 km per pixel, with a large shield volcano at the left-hand end and the Valles Marineris canyon system across the right, and a dark horizontal band running through the middle. The PDS dataset description states plainly that the dark west to east bands in sessions 3 and 4 are the shadow of Phobos.
credit: Don P. Mitchell (image processing), mentallandscape.com; original data Термоскан, ИКИ АН СССР, via NSSDC

mission_name: Space Exploration Initiative: the Mars element
caption: A black and white photograph of President George H. W. Bush speaking from the presidential podium on an outdoor stage at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington on 20 July 1989, at the ceremony marking the twentieth anniversary of the Apollo 11 landing. A very large United States flag hangs behind the stage with a Saturn V model standing beside it, and the platform party, which included the Apollo 11 crew, Vice President Dan Quayle and NASA Administrator Richard Truly, is applauding. NASA's own caption records that this is where Bush announced the Space Exploration Initiative.

mission_name: Space Exploration Initiative: the Mars element
caption: A 1989 NASA painting signed BOSSINAS '89 and numbered CD-89-41656, showing a blunt cone-shaped crewed Mars lander standing on legs and marked United States with the NASA worm logo, four suited astronauts at work, laid-out blue solar array blankets, an open-frame rover and an instrument package on the ground, under a deep red sky.
credit: NASA / Les Bossinas, NASA Lewis Research Center, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: Space Exploration Initiative: the Mars element
caption: A NASA artist's concept by Pat Rawlings of two suited astronauts and a rover on the rim of Noctis Labyrinthus in the Valles Marineris canyon system just after sunrise, with early morning cloud filling the canyon floor four miles below. NASA's caption dates the artwork to January 1989 and records that it was part of a NASA new initiatives study which surveyed possible future manned planetary expeditionary activity.
credit: NASA / Pat Rawlings, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: Space Exploration Initiative: the Mars element
caption: A NASA artist's concept by Paul DiMare of astronauts on Mars during a dust storm, with one helmet filling the left of the frame, a second suited figure walking across a boulder field and a wheeled pressurised vehicle with its lights on standing on a ridge behind them. NASA's caption records that the artwork was part of a NASA new initiatives study that surveyed possible future human planetary expeditions and dates it to 1989.
credit: NASA / Paul DiMare, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: A period NASA line drawing of the MESUR mission profile, running clockwise through the labels Launch, Probe Release, Independent Freeflight to Mars, Cruise Stage Separation and Entry, Parachute Release and Aeroshell Separation, and Instrument Deployment and Surface Operations, and ending with the disc-shaped MESUR station on the ground, mast raised, with MESUR and the NASA insignia on its side.
credit: NASA, as credited by SEIS/InSight (Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris, site by P. Labrot)

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: An artist's painting of the NetLander arrival, showing every stage of one descent at once: the conical entry shell falling away at upper left, three parachutes lowering ribbed capsules, a capsule bouncing across the ground on its airbags, and at lower right a landed station with its solar petals folded out and its instrument masts up.
credit: © CNES / ill. David Ducros, via SEIS/InSight (IPGP)

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: A studio photograph of the evacuated sphere built to house the SEIS seismometer for NetLander, opened into its two halves: on the left the empty upper dome, lined with gold-coloured segmented panels, and on the right the lower half holding the machined sensor support frame, blue-collared mounts and a flexible printed circuit.

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: An artist's painting of the CNES Mars Premier orbiter approaching Mars with its thrusters firing, its gold-blanketed body ringed by four brown conical NetLander entry capsules, three blue solar wings extended and a large pale disc across the back of the spacecraft. The SEIS/InSight caption describes it as the Mars Premier orbiter carrying the NetLander modules.
credit: © CNES / ill. David Ducros, via SEIS/InSight (IPGP)

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: A Russian-labelled diagram of the MetNet landing sequence, following the small meteorological station from separation from the carrier (Отделение ММС от КА) through opening of the first inflatable braking unit and atmospheric entry, deployment of the second inflatable unit, braking, ground contact (Касание ММС грунта) and finally the station in its working position with its mast raised.
credit: НПО им. С.А. Лавочкина (NPO Lavochkin), via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: The Mars networks that were never built
caption: A photograph taken at the Paris Air and Space Show at Le Bourget in June 2005 of a full-scale prototype suspended above a Russian aerospace stand, a wide white inflated braking cone with a copper-coloured instrument body slung beneath it and industry banners behind. RussianSpaceWeb's page states that NPO Lavochkin demonstrated this full-scale prototype of the device, which became known as MetNet, at Le Bourget in June 2005; it was the landing vehicle for the Mars-NET network mission, developed with the Finnish Meteorological Institute.
The Commercial Titan III lifting off from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station on 25 September 1992 carrying Mars Observer and the Transfer Orbit Stage, whose maiden flight this was.

Mars Observer mated to its Transfer Orbit Stage in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility on 13 August 1992, ready for encapsulation in the Titan III nose fairing; the gold-foiled instrument module and the high gain antenna dish are visible.
A JPL artist's concept of Mars Observer in Mars orbit with its six-panel solar array deployed. No photograph of the spacecraft at Mars exists, because it was lost 68 hours before orbit insertion.

A Mars Observer Camera narrow-angle frame taken at 00:52:47 UT on 14 April 1993 during cruise, showing part of Jupiter's disc with the moons Europa and Ganymede; the camera was still being focused, so the objects are blurred.

A colour photograph taken in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 19 August 1996, showing the Mars Orbiter Camera being lowered on a crane towards the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft while gowned technicians on a work platform guide it into place and others watch from the floor. NASA's caption records the camera as one of a suite of six instruments and gives the launch period as opening 6 November 1996.

A colour photograph of 14 September 1998 showing Mars Climate Orbiter suspended on a crane above its opened shipping container in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center. The blanketed spacecraft box carries the NASA meatball, a Lockheed Martin logo and a JPL logo side by side, and the container below it is stencilled with the Mars Surveyor '98 triangular mission patch and the words Mars '98 Orbiter.

A colour photograph of 22 October 1998 showing Mars Polar Lander on its workstand in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center during testing of the science instruments and spacecraft subsystems. The gold-blanketed lander deck, the stowed solar panels, the three landing legs and the white conical backshell above the deck are all visible, with one gowned technician working on the deck from a step platform.

A colour photograph of a Boeing Delta II lifting off from Launch Complex 17A at Cape Canaveral Air Station with Mars Climate Orbiter aboard at 1:45:51 p.m. EST on 11 December 1998. NASA's caption notes that the launch had slipped one day after a battery-related software problem was found in the spacecraft, and describes the orbiter as the first of the two Mars Surveyor '98 spacecraft.

A colour photograph of 13 March 2001 showing the 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center with the three panels of its solar array opened out ahead of illumination testing, the gold-blanketed spacecraft bus and high-gain dish behind the array, and eight gowned workers standing around it. NASA's caption lists its three instruments as THEMIS, the Gamma Ray Spectrometer and MARIE, and gives the launch date as 7 April 2001.

A colour photograph of a Mars Surveyor 2001 lander standing on three white test stands in a bare high-bay cell, its circular equipment deck wrapped in gold and silver thermal blanketing with amber plumbing and cabling running across it, protective yellow tape and red covers on the deck edge, and camera tripods and ground support cabling on the floor around it. JPL published it in a gallery headed ATLO Test and Integration Images on the lander's own site, with no individual caption and no date.
credit: NASA/JPL, Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

caption: A close colour photograph taken under the rim of the lander deck, showing gold multilayer insulation folded back over tanks and lines, a cluster of small rocket nozzles pointing down at the centre of the frame, valve and connector blocks bolted to the underside, and white cable harness taped across the structure. It is one of four frames JPL published without captions in the ATLO Test and Integration Images gallery.
credit: NASA/JPL, Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

caption: A labelled computer rendering of the 2001 lander's science deck seen from above and to one side, with white pointer arrows naming the Martian Radiation Environment Experiment (MARIE), Mini-TES, the APEX Pancam on its mast, the Mars In Situ Propellant Production experiment (MIP), the Mars Environmental Compatibility Assessment (MECA) and a Mossbauer Spectrometer, with two solar panels and the rover deployment ramp cut off at the edges of the frame. The rendering was made for the mission website, and the page that carries it credits the site's 2001 artwork to Corby J. Waste of JPL.
credit: NASA/JPL, Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine. The source page credits the site's 2001 artwork to Corby J. Waste, JPL.

caption: Museum object photography of the Marie Curie rover on its black plinth at the National Air and Space Museum, three-quarter view from the front left, showing the black solar panel with its colour calibration targets along the edge, the gold-foiled warm electronics box, the rocker-bogie suspension and all six cleated aluminium wheels. Part of the plinth label reading SOJOURNER FLIGHT SPARE MARIE C is visible at bottom left.
credit: Smithsonian Institution, National Air and Space Museum, via the Digital Public Library of America and Wikimedia Commons (CC0). The source record credits the photograph to Eric Long, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2018-10769); the object's creator is recorded as the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

caption: The Marie Curie rover as displayed at the National Air and Space Museum, standing on a pink plinth against a painted Martian backdrop with a larger rover model behind it. The exhibit label in the foreground is headed Marie Curie Rover, Sojourner's Flight Spare, and its text records that Sojourner landed on 4 July 1997 and operated for 85 days, that the rover shown is Sojourner's flight spare, and that the object was transferred from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
credit: Smithsonian Institution, National Air and Space Museum, via the Digital Public Library of America and Wikimedia Commons (CC0). The source record credits the photograph to Jim Preston, chief photographer, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2022-05070); the object's creator is recorded as the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology.

caption: A colour photograph released by JPL as PIA01885, showing the Phoenix Mars Lander partway through assembly and testing at Lockheed Martin Space Systems in Denver in September 2006, the lander deck on a work fixture in the clean room with its two circular solar arrays unfolded flat on either side and three gowned technicians working over the deck.

The Mars 96 orbiter standing on its handling ring in an assembly hall, solar panels partly deployed and the large spherical propellant tanks visible around its base, with a man at lower left giving the scale.
credit: No photographer credited. Published without an author line in NASA's Solar System Exploration image gallery (gallery date 26 June 2004). The spacecraft was built by NPO Lavochkin (НПО имени С.А. Лавочкина).

caption: Engineering model of one of the two Mars 96 small surface stations with its petals opened, on display in a case at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum's Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center; one of the four instrument slots holds the backup of JPL's Mars Oxidation Experiment, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory transferred the object to the museum in 2001.
credit: Sanjay Acharya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

caption: Line drawing of the Mars 96 orbiter in three views, showing the deployed solar panels, the dish antenna, the boom-mounted instruments and the spherical propellant tanks of the propulsion unit.
credit: No draughtsman credited. Reproduced in NASA/JPL's 1996 Mars Missions press kit, November 1996. The spacecraft was built by NPO Lavochkin (НПО имени С.А. Лавочкина) for the Space Research Institute (IKI) of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

caption: Jet Propulsion Laboratory workers in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center prepare Mars Global Surveyor, already mated to its solid propellant upper stage, for transfer to the launch pad on 21 October 1996.
Technicians in clean-room suits install the Mars Orbiter Camera on Mars Global Surveyor in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 19 August 1996.

Two global false-colour orthographic topographic maps of Mars built from Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter ranging, released in January 2001, showing the Tharsis rise and Valles Marineris on the left hemisphere and the Hellas basin on the right.

Two Mars Orbiter Camera views of a gully on the wall of an unnamed crater in Terra Sirenum at 36.6 degrees south, 161.8 degrees west, taken on 22 December 2001 and 26 August 2005; a light-toned deposit present in the later frame is absent from the earlier one.
A JPL artist's concept of Mars Global Surveyor flying over Mars, showing the high gain antenna on its boom and the two solar arrays that also served as aerobrakes.

A section of the geometrically improved, colour enhanced version of the Gallery Pan, taken by the Imager for Mars Pathfinder over sols 8, 9 and 10, showing Sojourner at the boulder Yogi with the lander's solar panel and deflated airbags in the foreground.

One of the first pictures taken by the Pathfinder lander's camera after touchdown at 10:07 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time on 4 July 1997, with Sojourner still stowed on a solar panel, deflated airbag material on either side, and two hills on the horizon.
A black and white Imager for Mars Pathfinder view taken on 7 July 1997 showing Sojourner on the surface with Barnacle Bill, the small rock at left, and Yogi, the large rock at upper right.
The first contiguous, uniform 360 degree colour panorama from the Imager for Mars Pathfinder, assembled from frames taken over sols 8, 9 and 10 with matched lighting and released on 22 July 1997.

A lander camera colour view of Sojourner on sol 22 near three small rocks nicknamed The Dice, with the alpha proton X-ray spectrometer at the rear of the rover and dark soil exposed in its wheel tracks.

An annotated HiRISE image from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, from the observation acquired on 21 December 2006, with yellow labels marking the Pathfinder lander, the backshell and parachute, and possible heat shield debris on the floor of Ares Vallis.

Jet Propulsion Laboratory technicians close the metal petals of the Mars Pathfinder lander in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility-2 at Kennedy Space Center on 2 October 1996, with Sojourner visible folded on one petal.

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: The rendered image released with the 20 July 1998 MAGE proposal announcement, showing the aircraft named Kitty Hawk banking above the canyons of Valles Marineris under an orange sky: a white swept-wing aeroplane with a rear-mounted pusher propeller behind a red spinner, twin canted tail surfaces, purple wingtips, the NASA insignia on the fin, USA and a United States flag on the wing, and KITTYHAWK lettered along the nose. The MSSS release calls it a simulated image.
credit: Malin Space Science Systems, for the MAGE proposal team (MSSS, NASA Ames Research Center, Naval Research Laboratory, Orbital Sciences Corporation)

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: The proposed MAGE survey route drawn on a Mars Digital Image Mosaic of Valles Marineris, three legs marked 800.0 km north to south in the west, 614.0 km east to west through the middle and 336.0 km north to south in the east, with an ellipse at the northern end representing the uncertainty in where the aircraft would be after entry and dashed lines showing the same route displaced within that ellipse.
credit: Malin Space Science Systems; base image the Mars Digital Image Mosaic (NASA, Viking)

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: NASA Langley artwork of the ARES Mars airplane, a white and blue rocket-powered aircraft with a twin-boom tail and the NASA insignia on its nose, banking low over cratered orange terrain. ARES is the Aerial Regional-scale Environmental Survey, the design that grew out of the cancelled 1999 Mars airplane micromission work.
credit: NASA Langley Research Center, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: A NASA engineering figure for the ARES entry, descent and deployment sequence. Four labelled renderings across the top show heat shield release, the Airplane Extraction System firing, extraction complete on the drogue riser and the wings deploying under the supersonic parachute. Below, an altitude against downrange plot traces the profile from 10 km to pullout complete with 3 sigma Monte Carlo scatter, beside a timeline table running from atmospheric interface at 135 km and Mach 24 to pullout complete at 2.41 km and Mach 0.64.
credit: NASA, via Wikimedia Commons; figure from NASA NTRS record 20080015501

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: A photograph of the half-scale ARES test aircraft, called the Mars Eagle, sitting on a wooden cradle on a foggy airfield with a Douglas DC-3 parked behind it. NASA's own caption reads ARES Mars Eagle on the morning of the high altitude drop test with DC-3 in background. The vehicle was carried by balloon to 103,500 feet and flown autonomously back down.

mission_name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
caption: Roughly sixty members of the ARES team at NASA Langley Research Center, all in blue ARES polo shirts, standing in ranks around a white and blue aircraft indoors, photographed from above. NASA's own caption reads Members of the ARES team posing with our full-scale drop-test airplane, and names nobody in the group.

The Nozomi spacecraft standing on a wheeled handling dolly stencilled PLANET-B in an ISAS clean room, its high-gain antenna dish and stowed solar paddles visible, with three engineers in clean room suits working around it. JAXA Digital Archives item P100006474.
credit: Provided by Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)

caption: Nozomi hardware, including its polished spherical propellant tanks, mounted on a stand inside a cylindrical space environment test chamber, with an engineer in a clean room suit standing beside it. JAXA Digital Archives material number P100006390, catalogued as 環境試験 (environmental testing).
credit: Provided by Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)

caption: A crescent Earth at lower left and the much smaller crescent Moon at upper right, seen together against black sky. Photographed by Nozomi and catalogued by JAXA as 「のぞみ」 地球と月, material number P100006058.
credit: Provided by Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA)

caption: The Mars Polar Lander stack at Kennedy Space Center in November 1998, its white backshell below and the copper-blanketed cruise stage above; the two Deep Space 2 probes are the dark units mounted on either side of the cruise stage.

A Jet Propulsion Laboratory worker in a clean room suit checks one of the Mars microprobes in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center, its aeroshell under a red protective cover.
The Deep Space 2 forebody, the 105.6 mm penetrator that carried the drill, sample chamber and laser water detector, photographed beside a wristwatch and a coin for scale.

Sarah Gavit, project manager for Deep Space 2 at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, photographed at a bench with a probe during final testing of the probes' electronics, before the aftbody cover was sewn up.

The Mars Surveyor '98 Climate Orbiter with technicians in a chamber during acoustic testing on 27 May 1998, a test that reproduces the sound levels of launch; the covered high gain antenna dish stands at the right of the spacecraft.
A technician works on Mars Climate Orbiter in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility-2 at Kennedy Space Center on 16 October 1998, about eight weeks before launch.

A Boeing Delta II lifts off from Launch Complex 17A at Cape Canaveral Air Station at 1:45:51 p.m. EST on 11 December 1998 carrying Mars Climate Orbiter, one day later than planned after a battery-related software problem was found in the spacecraft.

The first and only view of Mars returned by Mars Climate Orbiter, taken by the Mars Color Imager on 7 September 1999 when the spacecraft was about 4.5 million kilometres from the planet; the released frame is only 200 by 200 pixels.

A Kennedy Space Center technician looks over the assembled Mars Polar Lander in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2, with the white conical backshell resting above it and the solar panels spread open to either side in their deployed position.

Close view of the Mars Polar Lander in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center, seen from below with the solar panels spread open and the gold thermal blanketing over the lander deck.
The Delta II 7425 lifting off from Launch Complex 17 at Cape Canaveral Air Station carrying Mars Polar Lander and the two Deep Space 2 microprobes.

mission_name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
caption: A Viking Biology Instrument in a display case at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, photographed against a blue wall: an open grey frame holding two polished cylindrical module assemblies side by side, wired and plumbed, with yellow labels reading MODULE ASSEMBLY - PYROLYSIS EXPERIMENT and MODULE ASSEMBLY - LABELED RELEASE EXPERIMENT. The photographer's description records that the instrument was developed by TRW in Cleveland and states that this is the only one left on Earth, the other two being on Mars.
credit: Tim Evanson (CC BY-SA 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
caption: A 1976 NASA line drawing of the Viking biology instrument with its casing cut away, labelling the surface distribution assembly and the pyrolitic release lamp on the upper deck and, on the two shelves below, the three experiments: pyrolitic release, gas exchange and labeled release, with the electronics subsystem to the right and the mechanical subsystem beneath. The drawing carries the original page number 36 and NASA's own spellings, pyrolitic and labled.
credit: NASA, from the 1976 Viking press material Vikings converge on Mars (NTRS 19760018033)

mission_name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
caption: A JPL artist's concept of the Astrobiology Field Laboratory: a six-wheel rocker-bogie rover with a gold-brown body, a grey high-gain dish and mast on the deck and two instrument arms reaching down, parked on pale layered sedimentary ground threaded with white mineral veins, dark buttes on the horizon. The image was published on JPL's Mars future missions page in the years when AFL was still in the plan. It is a painting of a rover that was never built.
credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech, artwork by Corby Waste (credit as given on the Wikimedia Commons file page)

mission_name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
caption: An artist's concept of the Icebreaker lander on rusty, stony ground with patches of pale ice at the edges of the frame: a Phoenix-derived platform on three legs with two circular fan-fold solar arrays, a small camera mast, and a slim vertical drill running down past the deck into the soil. The Planetary Society captions it as an artist's concept of the Mars Icebreaker Life spacecraft. No Icebreaker lander was ever built.

mission_name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
caption: Three labelled photographs from the September 2019 Atacama Rover Astrobiology Drilling Studies field campaign in northern Chile. Panel A shows the four-wheeled KREX2 test rover on desert gravel with its parts called out: lidar, navigation cameras, the Honeybee Robotics TRIDENT drill standing vertically at the rear, the blue robotic arm, sample funnels and the instrument bay. Panels B and C show the arm and scoop deployed under the drill and a close-up of the cog wheel that pushes cuttings off the auger flights into the scoop. The paper records that TRIDENT was also selected for the proposed Icebreaker mission.
credit: Carol R. Stoker et al., Astrobiology 23(12), 2023, via PubMed Central (CC BY 4.0)

caption: Roughly fifty members of the ARES team in matching blue ARES polo shirts, packed shoulder to shoulder around a full-scale ARES test airplane indoors at NASA Langley, the aircraft finished in white with dark blue sweeps and a United States flag on its tail fin. The Commons file page identifies team leader Joel S. Levine at the bottom right. This airframe is a ground test article built at Langley, and no ARES was ever built to go to Mars.

The half-scale ARES drop-test aircraft, which the project called the Mars Eagle, sitting on a wooden cradle on a fog-bound airfield apron with its wings and tail deployed, white with orange wingtips and tail, cables trailing across the tarmac, and a Douglas DC-3 parked behind it. The project's multimedia page captions the frame as the ARES Mars Eagle on the morning of the high altitude drop test with a DC-3 in the background.

A frame from the tail-mounted video camera of the half-scale Mars Eagle during its 19 September 2002 high-altitude flight, looking forward along a deployed wing and the twin tail booms towards a black sky and the curved bright limb of the Earth, with cloud and terrain far below. The project's multimedia page captions it as the ARES Mars Eagle descending over Oregon during its high altitude flight test.

A bare metal ARES wind-tunnel model mounted upside down on a yellow-taped sting inside NASA Langley's Transonic Dynamics Tunnel, wings and tail in their fully deployed positions, rows of pressure taps drilled into the wing, tunnel lights burning through portholes in the wall behind it. The project's multimedia page captions the frame as the current ARES wind tunnel model in the TDT in May 2004.

The entry, descent and deployment figure from the 2006 ARES proposal documentation. Four CAD panels across the top show the folded airplane still inside the backshell at heat shield release, the release pyros firing, extraction complete on the drogue riser, and the wings deploying beneath the supersonic parachute. Below them an altitude against downrange plot traces the whole sequence with three sigma Monte Carlo boxes, and a table lists every event from atmospheric interface at 135 km and Mach 24 to pullout complete at 2.41 km and Mach 0.64, 309 seconds later. It is an engineering drawing of a vehicle that was never built.
credit: NASA, from Design of the ARES Mars Airplane and Mission Architecture (NTRS 20080015501)

caption: A NASA Langley artist's concept of the drogue chute and tail deployment step, drawn over cratered Martian highlands. A dark truss, the airplane extraction structure, hangs beneath the white drogue canopy at the upper left with its own risers running up out of frame; a single line runs down from the canopy to the aircraft, and the aircraft itself is shown with its tail unfolded but its wings still folded flat down against the fuselage. The backshell is not in frame. The project's own multimedia page labels this image an artist's concept of ARES during drogue chute and tail deployment.

mission_name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
caption: The title graphic from the PADME proposal, headed with the NASA insignia, PADME, and Phobos And Deimos & Mars Environment. A rendering of the LADEE derived spacecraft, an octagonal bus with body mounted solar panels and a high gain horn on top, is montaged between a small Deimos at the upper left, a large cratered Phobos at the lower left and a bright orange Mars filling the right hand side.
credit: Pascal Lee and colleagues, NASA Ames Research Center, from LPSC 2014 abstract 2288; via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
caption: A labelled proposal diagram headed MERLIN, Two Views of Spacecraft Show Science and Exploration Payload. The upper view names the orbital instruments, an orbital imaging system, a dust particle counter, a radiation monitor marked not visible and a deep space optical communication terminal. The lower view has the robotic arm raised and points to a turret carrying an alpha particle X-ray spectrometer and a microscopic imaging spectrometer, a mini gamma ray spectrometer on the forearm, and a landed stereo camera.
credit: MERLIN Team / JHUAPL, via The Planetary Society

mission_name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
caption: A concept rendering headed Landing Enables Robust Science, showing the gold wrapped MERLIN spacecraft standing on four legs on the grey cratered surface of Phobos with a large crescent Mars behind it, its dish antenna up and two solar wings out, and yellow labels pointing to the robotic arm with contact instruments and the stereo imager.
credit: MERLIN Team / JHUAPL, via The Planetary Society

mission_name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
caption: An artist's concept, marked Artist's concept in its lower left corner, of a spiked hedgehog robot lying on the grey dusty slope of a small cratered body, with Mars large in the black sky above it, so the body shown is one of the two Martian moons. It is the lead image on JPL's 3 September 2015 release about the hedgehog robots, which JPL, Stanford and MIT developed jointly.

mission_name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
caption: A photograph of a built hedgehog prototype standing on a white surface: an open aluminium cube frame with cross braced faces, internal flywheels visible through the openings, one face marked +X, and carbon fibre spikes tipped with white balls projecting from every corner. JPL's caption, dated 10 July 2014, calls it a hopping and tumbling robot that scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory will test on a parabolic aircraft flight.

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: The Marie Curie rover on a magenta display plinth at the National Air and Space Museum, standing on six cleated aluminium wheels with the rocker bogie linkage and the gold warm electronics box under the flat solar panel, a strip of colour reference chips along the panel edge, and a museum label in front of it headed Marie Curie Rover, Sojourner's Flight Spare and footed Transferred from National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
credit: Photo by Jim Preston, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2022-05070); rover object A20150317000, transferred from NASA; via Wikimedia Commons, CC0

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: The same rover photographed from below the solar panel, showing the gold foil warm electronics box, bundles of white and coloured wiring and connectors along the chassis, a small mission decal on the box side, a cylindrical instrument head at the right hand end and all six cleated wheels on their rocker bogie linkage. Part of a Pathfinder lander display and a Mars backdrop stand behind it.
credit: Photo by Eric Long, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2018-10772); rover object A20150317000, transferred from NASA; via Wikimedia Commons, CC0

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: Figure 7 of the MetNet team's own 2017 paper, two photographs of built MetNet hardware side by side. On the left the surface module with its conical forebody pushed out of the telescopic tube on its spring. On the right the internal body with the equipment module mounted below it, standing on the six hollow shock absorbing tubes that flatten as they slide through undersized slots in the flanges and so soak up the landing impact.
credit: A.-M. Harri and colleagues, The MetNet vehicle: a lander to deploy environmental stations for local and global investigations of Mars, Geoscientific Instrumentation, Methods and Data Systems 6, 103 to 124, 2017, Figure 7, CC BY 3.0

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: A full scale lander article hanging on a Russian industry stand at an air show, its inflatable braking system fully deployed: a white fabric tension cone roughly two metres across, a gold and dark brown toroidal rim carrying the flexible heat shield around its edge, and the copper coloured penetrator body slung below on a cylinder. RussianSpaceWeb captions it as a lander with an inflatable heat shield for the Mars-NET mission, shown at Le Bourget in 2005.

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: A computer rendering of the Canadian Northern Light lander on an orange Martian plain under a dust coloured sky: a low three lobed body with a solar panel on each lobe and a jointed arm reaching out and down with an instrument head on the end. The Commons file page describes it as an artist's impression of the lander with its robotic arm deployed to search for evidence of photosynthetic life, dated 2009 and credited to Air Whistle Media for Thoth Technology.
credit: Air Whistle Media / Thoth Technology Inc., uploaded to Wikimedia Commons by Ben Quine, CC BY-SA 3.0

mission_name: The Mars hardware with no ride
caption: The 46 m steerable dish at the Algonquin Radio Observatory in Ontario, tilted up against a clear sky above bare spring bush, its white panelled surface, tripod feed support and quadrupod bracing all visible. The Commons file page dates the photograph to 29 April 2013, gives the site coordinates, and describes the antenna as the largest fully steerable one in Canada. The photographer, Ben Quine, was Northern Light's principal investigator.
credit: Ben Quine (Wikimedia Commons user Bquine), CC BY-SA 3.0

caption: A HiRISE image from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing Phoenix hanging beneath its parachute during descent on 25 May 2008, with a 10 km crater informally named Heimdall filling the frame behind it and a full-resolution inset of the parachute and lander at lower left. JPL's caption notes that although Phoenix appears to be descending into the crater it is actually about 20 km in front of it.

A colour photograph of 23 August 2013 showing the MAVEN spacecraft standing on its rotation fixture inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center ahead of testing and launch preparations, its instrument booms and blanketed bus exposed and its solar arrays not yet fitted. Mission plaques for NASA, Mars Global Surveyor, Stardust and Mars Science Laboratory hang on the wall behind it.
credit: NASA/Chris Rhodes, as given in NASA's own caption (KSC-2013-3455)

caption: A colour photograph of the ARES Mars Eagle, the half-scale drop-test aeroplane, sitting on a wooden cradle on wet tarmac in fog with its wings spread and red-tipped, a vertical tail below the fuselage and a silver DC-3 parked behind it. NASA Langley's own caption for the frame reads: ARES Mars Eagle on the morning of the high altitude drop test with DC-3 in background.
credit: NASA Langley Research Center, ARES project website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

caption: An onboard video frame looking forward along the wing of the ARES Mars Eagle in flight, with the curve of the Earth's limb and the dark sky of the upper atmosphere across the top of the picture and cloud and terrain far below. NASA Langley's own caption for the frame reads: ARES Mars Eagle descending over Oregon during its high altitude flight test.
credit: NASA Langley Research Center, ARES project website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

caption: An artist's rendering released by JPL as PIA07085 under the title Concept for Mars Volcanic Emission Life Scout, showing a three-panel orbiter above a dark Martian landscape with instrument sight lines reaching down to a glowing vent and a circular inset detail of a fissure in the ground. NASA's own summary describes it as an artist's rendition of a concept for a Mars orbiter that would scrutinise the atmosphere for chemical traces of life or of environments that could support life.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey orbiter, wrapped in gold thermal blanket and slung from an overhead crane, is lowered onto a workstand in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 at Kennedy Space Center on 5 January 2001 while the processing team checks its position.

A false colour panorama of the Martian horizon built from three infrared channels of the THEMIS camera, one of ten shot on 9 May 2023 from about 400 km up after engineers rolled Odyssey nearly 90 degrees.

Odyssey's global map of intermediate-energy (epithermal) neutrons from its first three months of mapping, in which deep blue marks a low neutron count and therefore hydrogen-rich soil, concentrated at both poles.
credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona/Los Alamos National Laboratories

caption: A Boeing Delta II lifts off from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station at 11:02 a.m. EDT on 7 April 2001 carrying 2001 Mars Odyssey, watched by crowds in the foreground.
An artist's concept showing 2001 Mars Odyssey in orbit above Mars with its three-panel solar array and the gamma ray sensor head extended on its 6 m boom.

A technician on a step ladder works on the foil-wrapped Mars Odyssey orbiter in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility 2 on 23 March 2001, shortly before the spacecraft was mated to the Delta II third stage.

A full-size replica of Beagle 2 on display at the Science Museum in London, opened out as the lander was meant to open on Mars: the gold bowl and its instrument deck at the back, the four solar panel petals laid flat around the central lid, and the robotic arm carrying the cameras and spectrometers.
credit: Photo by Wikimedia Commons user geni, CC BY-SA 4.0

caption: The mission's own publicity image: a full-size mock-up of Beagle 2 fully deployed on a studio set built to look like the Martian surface, showing the four solar panels, the lid-mounted panel, the base and the PAW instrument arm at right.
credit: All Rights Reserved Beagle 2, via ESA

caption: Colin Pillinger of the Open University, who talked ESA into carrying a British lander and then spent years raising the money for it, photographed at Jodrell Bank on 19 July 2009 with the crutches and mobility scooter he used after his multiple sclerosis diagnosis.
credit: Mike Peel; Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics, University of Manchester, CC BY-SA 4.0

caption: The Mars Express Visual Monitoring Camera looking back at Beagle 2 about a minute after the spring ejection on 19 December 2003, with the lander appearing as the single overexposed white dot at the left edge of an otherwise black frame, roughly 20 m away.
The clinching colour HiRISE observation of 15 December 2014, in which a bright feature a couple of metres across in Isidis Planitia is labelled as Beagle 2, with a 10 m scale bar for reference.
credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Univ. of Arizona/University of Leicester (the image itself is captioned HiRISE/NASA/Leicester)

caption: An annotated HiRISE frame from 29 June 2014 boxing three features on the floor of Isidis Planitia interpreted as the Beagle 2 lander, a probable parachute and the rear cover, spread over a few hundred metres.
credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Univ. of Arizona/University of Leicester (the image itself is captioned University of Leicester/Beagle 2/NASA/JPL/University of Arizona)

caption: A composite of two HiRISE observations, enlarged and enhanced, in which Beagle 2 resolves into a small cluster of bright points rather than a single dot, the reading that led the team to conclude that the solar panels had partly opened.
credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Univ. of Arizona/University of Leicester (the image itself is captioned HiRISE/NASA/JPL/Parker/Leicester)

caption: An artist's impression of Mars Express over Mars, composited by ESA onto a real High Resolution Stereo Camera image of the planet taken by the spacecraft itself.
credit: Spacecraft image credit: ESA/ATG medialab; Mars: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin

caption: The flight spacecraft, gold thermal blanket showing, sits on top of the white Fregat upper stage inside the processing hall at Baikonur Cosmodrome in May 2003, surrounded by yellow access scaffolding.
The Soyuz-Fregat carrying Mars Express and Beagle 2 lifts off from Baikonur Cosmodrome on 2 June 2003 at 23:45 local time.

A High Resolution Stereo Camera swath taken on 19 October 2023 during orbit 25,000, showing Olympus Mons at upper left, the three Tharsis Montes running down the middle, the head of Valles Marineris at lower right, and Phobos as a small dark spot near the bottom left.

A computer-generated perspective view looking north-east over Tithonium and Ius Chasma at the western end of Valles Marineris, built from High Resolution Stereo Camera stereo data taken on 26 May 2004 during orbit 442 at about 52 m per pixel.

An ESA computer-generated visualisation of Mars Express with the second 20 m MARSIS glass-fibre boom extended, issued alongside the 14 June 2005 deployment. Mars Express carried no camera able to see its own booms, so the deployment was confirmed from spacecraft telemetry and dynamics, not from any picture. The deployment had been postponed for a year over fears the booms could snap back into the spacecraft.

The JPL artist's concept released on 29 March 2005 as PIA07500, titled Mars Telecommunications Orbiter, Artist's Concept, showing the spacecraft in front of Mars with a gold-blanketed bus, a large white high-gain dish, two long solar wings, a cylindrical optical terminal assembly on top and a flat radiator panel below.

The JPL artist's concept released on 29 March 2005 as PIA07499, titled Mars Laser Communication Demonstration, Artist Concept, showing the Mars Telecommunications Orbiter above Mars with a red beam running from the small optical terminal on its upper deck all the way to Earth. NASA's caption describes it as a concept for operation of an optical communications system on the orbiter, with the primary work left to the radio link.

A JPL graphic released on 29 November 2016 as PIA21139, Strengthening the Mars Telecommunications Network, showing the geometry of the rover Opportunity transmitting UHF data up to ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter, whose long elliptical orbit is drawn in red around the planet. The orbiter received the data on one of its NASA-supplied Electra UHF radios and relayed it to Earth on its own X-band link.

PIA17759, a vertical-projection Pancam self-portrait assembled from frames taken 3 to 6 January 2014, about three weeks before Opportunity completed ten years on Mars, with dust still coating the solar arrays after a partial wind cleaning.

PIA05755, the Lion King panorama: an approximate true-colour Pancam mosaic of 558 frames taken on sols 58 and 60 showing Eagle crater, the discarded lander, the bedrock outcrop in the crater wall, and the plains of Meridiani Planum beyond.
PIA19113, a microscopic imager close-up taken beside Fram crater on sol 84, 19 April 2004, with colour added from the panoramic camera; the area shown is about 3 centimetres across.

PIA07110, an approximately true-colour Pancam mosaic of Burns Cliff on the inner southeastern wall of Endurance crater, composited from 46 image sets taken over sols 287 to 294, 13 to 20 November 2004.
PIA09104, a Pancam vista of Victoria crater taken from the promontory called Cape Verde, assembled from hundreds of exposures acquired between sols 970 and 991, 16 October to 7 November 2006.

PIA14509, a Pancam mosaic recorded after Opportunity reached the rim of Endeavour crater on 9 August 2011, showing the Spirit Point area of the rim, the small crater Odyssey, and the interior of Endeavour beyond.

PIA22909, the approximately true-colour version of Opportunity's last panorama: 354 Pancam frames taken in Perseverance Valley between sols 5,084 and 5,111, 13 May to 10 June 2018, with a group of frames at lower left that were never filled in through the green and violet filters before the dust storm ended the mission.

PIA03275, a polar-projection mosaic that combines a self-portrait of Spirit's deck with the 360-degree panorama the rover shot from the true summit of Husband Hill over sols 583 to 586, 24 to 27 August 2005.
PIA03095, the Everest Panorama: an approximately true-colour 360-degree Pancam mosaic taken from the true summit of Husband Hill in the Columbia Hills over sols 620 to 622, 1 to 3 October 2005.

PIA11758, an approximately true-colour Pancam mosaic from sol 1202, 21 May 2007, showing the bright trench of soil turned over by Spirit's inoperable right front wheel at the patch nicknamed Gertrude Weise, east of Home Plate.

PIA12002, a black and white wide-angle view from Spirit's front hazard-avoidance camera on sol 1889, 26 April 2009, showing the soil churned up by two short backward drives that slipped, with Husband Hill on the horizon.

PIA12203, the Calypso Panorama: a full-circle Pancam mosaic assembled from hundreds of frames taken between sols 1906 and 1943, 14 May to 20 June 2009, from the embedded rover's position at Troy, with the west edge of Home Plate filling the right half and Husband Hill in the distance near the centre.
PIA10128, a vertical-projection Pancam self-portrait of Spirit's deck built from frames taken over sols 1355 to 1358, 26 to 29 October 2007, showing the solar arrays under a heavy coat of dust.

Technicians in cleanroom garments work on the Spirit rover during final checkout in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 28 March 2003, with the STS-107 memorial plaque visible mounted on the rover's high-gain antenna.
credit: NASA/KSC (the source record names no individual photographer)

caption: A crop of the USGS gazetteer's MC-13 Syrtis Major quadrangle sheet, THEMIS imagery tinted by MOLA elevation and overprinted with IAU-approved names only: Antoniadi, Baldet, Flammarion, Leighton, Jezero, Nili Fossae, Syrtis Major Planum, Isidis Planitia, Terra Sabaea, Arena Colles, Libya Montes, and in the lower right the small craters Bradbury, Woking, Yalgoo, Chupadero, Ohara, Beruri, Dubois and Nashir.
credit: NASA and the Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature, IAU Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature (WGPSN), via Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

caption: The framed Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station plaque held by the National Air and Space Museum, shown beside the document of 18 May 1984 by which NASA administrator James M. Beggs transferred the Viking 1 lander on Mars to the museum and charged it to retain, secure and protect the plaque. The plaque is headed Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station, reads "Dedicated to the memory of Tim Mutch" and continues about his imagination, verve and resolve, is signed by administrator Robert A. Frosch and dated January 7, 1981, and ends with a line marked Emplaced that has been left blank.
credit: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, photograph by Mark Avino (NASM2026-01015)
