caption: The aluminium memorial plaque to the STS-107 crew, roughly six inches across and designed by JPL engineers Chris Voorhees and Peter Illsley, mounted on the back of Spirit's high-gain antenna and photographed by the rover's navigation camera on the surface of Mars. It carries a shuttle silhouette, the words IN MEMORIAM, the seven names, a NASA insignia and a United States flag, with the plain of Gusev crater behind it. JPL released the frame on 7 January 2004.

A Spirit panoramic camera view east across Gusev crater, released by JPL under the title NASA Dedicates Mars Landmarks to Columbia Crew, with the low ridge on the horizon labelled Columbia Hills Complex and each of its seven summits named for a member of the STS-107 crew: Anderson, Brown, Chawla, Clark, Husband, Mc Cool and Ramon, with the azimuth and range of each from the rover, between 2.9 and 4.4 km. Spirit's deflated airbags fill the bottom of the frame.

A HiRISE orbital image of the floor of Gale crater with Curiosity's first four months of driving plotted on it: yellow waypoint markers, a traverse path, a dashed outline marking the descent blast zone, and the sites labelled Bradbury Landing at the west end, then Rocknest, Point Lake, Glenelg and Yellowknife Bay to the east. The markings are drawn on; the terrain beneath them is the photograph.

The first colour photograph taken from an aircraft on another world, made by Ingenuity's colour camera on 22 April 2021 during its second flight while the helicopter was about 5.2 m above the ground. Two of its landing feet appear at the left and right edges, its shadow falls at bottom centre, and the parallel treads of Perseverance's wheels cross the surface. NASA's caption places Wright Brothers Field in the vicinity of the shadow.

mission_name: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
caption: A Spirit panoramic camera image taken on 2 February 2004, sol 30, showing the rover's arm turret against the ground of Gusev crater, with the cylindrical cable guard of the rock abrasion tool at the upper left carrying an image of the United States flag. The shield was machined from aluminium recovered from the World Trade Center site.

mission_name: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
caption: A combined view taken by Opportunity on 11 September 2011, sol 2,713, in which a colour panoramic camera frame of the rover's arm turret is inset into a wider grey navigation camera frame of the ground. The flag on the rock abrasion tool's cable guard is at the centre of the colour inset.

mission_name: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
caption: A close view of the rock abrasion tool on a full-scale Mars Exploration Rover display model at the Virginia Air and Space Center, photographed in July 2010, with the grinding head, the brush and the flag-marked cylindrical cable guard all visible at arm's length against a simulated Martian floor.
credit: Rtphokie, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

caption: An artist's concept of Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter over the Nilosyrtis region with its high-gain antenna, twin solar arrays and instrument deck facing the surface.

Lockheed Martin technicians on work platforms prepare a full range-of-motion gimbal test of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter high-gain antenna in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 25 May 2005.
Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter lifts off at 7:43 a.m. EDT on 12 August 2005 on a Lockheed Martin Atlas V from Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, NASA's first use of the Atlas V.

HiRISE catches the Perseverance descent stage falling through the Martian atmosphere under its parachute on 18 February 2021, shot from about 700 km away while MRO was moving at roughly 3 km per second, with the Jezero delta at left.

HiRISE observation ESP_069665_2055, acquired 6 June 2021 at about 29 cm per pixel, showing China's Tianwen-1 landing platform as the bright spot at the centre of a dark blast pattern in southern Utopia Planitia, with the Zhurong rover as a smaller bright spot just to the south.

HiRISE view of 25 October 2016 showing the ground where ESA's Schiaparelli test lander struck Meridiani Planum on 19 October 2016, with magnified insets of the three sites where separate components of the spacecraft hit.

Dark narrow streaks known as recurring slope lineae running down the walls of Garni Crater, shown on a HiRISE digital terrain model with the vertical scale exaggerated, published in September 2015 when NASA presented them as evidence of present-day briny water.

A photograph looking down the length of the NEK hall at the Institute of Biomedical Problems in Moscow, showing the linked pressure modules of the Mars500 facility from outside: a dark red barrel-vaulted module in the foreground, bare metal cylinders behind it ringed with red-painted clamps, walkways and stairs alongside, and a run of sponsor and media boards fixed to the gallery on the right.

The six-man 520-day crew in blue MARS 500 coveralls on the steps outside the modules, photographed by ESA just before they entered the facility at 13:49 local time in Moscow on 3 June 2010, with one man waving.

A man in a green Institute of Biomedical Problems flight suit stands on the access platform in the open outer doorway of the module marked ЭУ 250, arms spread wide, while photographers and staff watch from below; ESA publishes the frame under the title Closing the hatch in June 2010 with a caption describing the 3 June 2010 start of the experiment. ESA does not name the man, so this entry does not either.

The simulated martian terrain hall at IBMP, a dark ribbed room about 10 m by 6 m floored with reddish sand and scattered pale rocks, with pinprick star lights set into the dark walls, a small wheeled rover parked at the back and a figure in a gold-coloured pressure suit carrying an ESA flag on a pole; observers in ordinary clothes stand in the doorway. ESA's own caption calls this training on the simulated terrain, which is a different event from the sealed February 2011 Marswalk, and the room was dressed to resemble the surface at Gusev crater.

A man in a green Institute of Biomedical Problems flight suit stands on the platform and works the handle of the heavy padded door of the ЭУ module, with a doctor in a white coat and another official waiting at the right of frame; ESA's caption reads Opening the door of the Mars500 facility after 520 days.

The four CHAPEA Mission 2 crew, James Spicer, Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery and Ellen Ellis, standing and sitting in front of a science glovebox inside the 3D-printed Mars Dune Alpha habitat at Johnson Space Center, the printed ribbing of the walls visible behind them and a rainforest print hung on the wall; NASA dates the frame 5 August 2026 and captions it as the crew marking 300 days inside.

mission_name: MAX-C and the Mars Exploration Joint Initiative
caption: A computer-aided design depiction of the proposed Mars Astrobiology Explorer-Cacher, taken from the MEPAG presentation of MAX-C to the planetary decadal survey dated 10 September 2009. The rover is shown with a camera head on a short mast, a jointed instrument arm folded at the left, a cluttered equipment deck and two large circular fan-shaped solar arrays carried out on booms, the solar power that confined the mission to latitudes between 25 degrees north and 15 degrees south.
credit: Lisa Pratt, Dave Beaty, Joy Crisp and Scott McLennan, NASA MEPAG, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: MAX-C and the Mars Exploration Joint Initiative
caption: An ESA render of the two rovers that were to be landed together on one NASA descent stage in 2018, published by BBC News on 7 April 2011 under the headline US and Europe mull single 2018 Mars rover. NASA's MAX-C stands at the left, identifiable by the pair of circular fan-shaped solar arrays on booms; ESA's ExoMars rover stands at the right with its flat rectangular panels, camera mast and drill box. The BBC caption reads that the idea was to send two rovers together, one from the US (Max-C), and one from Europe (ExoMars).
credit: ESA (watermarked on the image), as published by BBC News

caption: The first Mars exploration aircraft airframe standing on a hangar floor: a straight high aspect ratio wing in taped panels resting on foam blocks, a slim black carbon fibre fuselage pod, a boom running back to a tailplane with twin fins, and no landing gear. The article's Figure 3 caption names it the first unit of the Mars exploration aircraft, the airframe carried to 36 km by balloon and released nose down.
credit: ISAS/JAXA, from Masayuki Anyoji, Space Science Frontline, 24 May 2017

caption: The balloon gondola for the June 2016 drop test, an aluminium frame box faced with orange and white chequered panels and a red beacon on one corner, hanging on lifting straps with the Mars aeroplane stowed inside it: the black fuselage hangs vertically down the middle with the white wing panels stacked behind it. The article's Figure 3 caption identifies it as the gondola with the airframe installed.
credit: ISAS/JAXA, from Masayuki Anyoji, Space Science Frontline, 24 May 2017

caption: The Mars atmospheric wind tunnel with the end of its vacuum chamber swung open: a large polished cylinder with its circular hatch standing back, and a square section suction wind tunnel with its test section mounted on a frame inside. The article's Figure 1 caption gives the chamber diameter as about 1.8 m and explains that a supersonic ejector downstream of the test section drives the flow by injecting high pressure gas.
credit: ISAS/JAXA, from Masayuki Anyoji, Space Science Frontline, 24 May 2017

caption: A black carbon fibre tandem wing test aircraft lying on grass and gravel, two straight wings one behind the other on a flat central body, twin vertical fins on the rear body, a slim nose boom and a trailing cable. sorae publishes it as the high altitude test vehicle for the Mars exploration aeroplane that the University of Tsukuba startup AeroFlex delivered to JAXA in October 2025, for a stratospheric flight test at about 30 km.
Surface Stereo Imager panorama looking out over the arctic plain, with one of the lander's circular solar panels in the foreground and the robotic arm holding a soil sample in its scoop.

HiRISE image from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing Phoenix descending under its parachute on 25 May 2008, with a large crater behind it. The lander and parachute are only a few pixels across at full scale, so NASA boxed them and repeated them enlarged in an inset at the lower left.
Robotic Arm Camera view underneath the lander on sol 5, framed by landing struts, showing the smooth bright patch left where the descent thrusters blew the loose soil aside.

Two Surface Stereo Imager frames of the Dodo-Goldilocks trench, labelled sol 20 and sol 24 (15 and 19 June 2008), in which a cluster of bright lumps in the lower left of the trench floor shrinks and disappears over four days. The larger bright patch higher up the trench is still there in both frames.
The floor of the trench informally named Snow White in July 2008, scored with rasp and scrape marks made in preparation for collecting a sample of the hard subsurface layer.

A lidar data plot rather than a photograph: the Canadian-built lidar on Phoenix profiling a cloud on sol 99, with labelled fall streaks of ice crystals descending from the cloud base near 4 km altitude.

The Delta II 7925 carrying Phoenix lifting off from Pad 17A at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station at 5:26 a.m. EDT on 4 August 2007, with the mission emblem visible on the rocket. NASA's own record for this frame credits the photographers Regina Mitchell-Ryall and Jerry Cannon.

The silica glass mini-DVD photographed against a plain background on Earth, its label reading Messages from Earth, Phoenix, 2007, Attention Astronauts: Take This with You, and at the foot Visions of Mars: First Library on Mars, with a painting of a row of old books at the left, a swirled Mars motif at the right, a paragraph of explanatory text below the hub, and the names of the University of Arizona, Lockheed Martin, NASA and JPL running around the rim.

The title screen of the Visions of Mars disc as The Planetary Society publishes it on its 2007 Phoenix credits page: a rendered Mars against black with the words Visions of Mars across it, ringed by the name of the planet written in a dozen other scripts, among them Sanskrit, Cyrillic, Korean, Chinese, Hebrew, Thai, Greek and Arabic.

A Surface Stereo Imager view down onto the Phoenix lander deck in the first days after landing, with the mini-DVD lying flat at the lower left, its label and the words Attention Astronauts: Take This with You legible, a small United States flag beside it, a solar panel at the upper left and the rock strewn arctic plain filling the rest of the frame.

A vertical projection assembled from hundreds of Surface Stereo Imager exposures, showing the whole Phoenix lander from overhead with both circular solar arrays spread, the instrument deck between them and the black disc where the camera's own mounting blocks the view. The mini-DVD is bolted to this deck, next to the small flag near the lower edge of the lander body.
The Zenit-2SB rocket carrying Phobos-Grunt standing floodlit on the pad at Site 45, Baikonur, on the night of the launch, 8 to 9 November 2011.

Liftoff of the Zenit-2SB with Phobos-Grunt and China's Yinghuo-1 microsatellite from Site 45 at Baikonur at 20:16:03 UTC on 8 November 2011, which was already past midnight in Moscow and four in the morning in Beijing.

The Phobos-Grunt flight spacecraft photographed fully assembled at NPO Lavochkin in Khimki, the four stacked vehicles standing together: the jettisonable propellant tank block, the main propulsion unit, the cruise and landing module, and the return vehicle with its re-entry capsule.
credit: НПО имени С.А. Лавочкина (NPO Lavochkin), via RussianSpaceWeb.com

caption: A Roscosmos display model of Phobos-Grunt at the 2011 Paris Air Show, numbered by the photographer to identify the drop tank, the cruise module, Yinghuo-1, the orbiter and lander, the Earth re-entry module and the sample capsule.
A half-second handheld exposure taken from Cornwall on the evening of 27 November 2011 showing Phobos-Grunt as a streak of light crossing Cygnus while stranded in low Earth orbit.
ESA's tracking station at Perth in Western Australia, showing the 15 metre main dish and the small secondary antenna above it that was used to command Phobos-Grunt.

A Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera image of Phobos at 8.2 metres per pixel from orbit 8974, with two ellipses drawn on it marking the earlier planned landing site in red and the site under consideration in blue for Phobos-Grunt.
credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin (G. Neukum), CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO

caption: SpaceX concept art titled Dragon to Mars, showing a Dragon capsule glowing white hot as it enters the martian atmosphere at hypersonic speed, dragging a long incandescent wake across the sunlit face of the planet with the canyon system of Valles Marineris below it.

SpaceX concept art of a Dragon 2 capsule a few metres above the martian surface with its four landing legs extended, SuperDraco engines firing from the pods set into its side walls and blasting grit horizontally across the ground.
SpaceX concept art of a landed Dragon capsule standing alone on its legs in a wide rock-strewn martian valley, small against the ridges and the dusty horizon.

SpaceX concept art of a Falcon Heavy with a Dragon capsule on top climbing away from launch complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in a bank of exhaust, posted to the Official SpaceX Photos Flickr account on 27 April 2016, the day SpaceX announced it would send Dragons to Mars as early as 2018.

PIA22207, a self-portrait of Curiosity standing on Vera Rubin Ridge, assembled from dozens of Mars Hand Lens Imager frames all taken on 23 January 2018, sol 1943, with the lower slopes of Aeolis Mons rising just behind the rover's mast and the rim of Gale crater on the horizon at both edges.

PIA15978, the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter catching the Mars Science Laboratory entry vehicle descending under its fully inflated parachute on 6 August 2012 UTC, with an inset cutout of the back shell stretched to avoid saturation.

The United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 rising from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral on 26 November 2011 with the Mars Science Laboratory spacecraft sealed inside its payload fairing. NASA's Kennedy Space Center media archive is the source; the file credits NASA without naming an individual photographer.
PIA16726, a Mars Hand Lens Imager view centred on the borehole Curiosity's drill cut into the mudstone slab called John Klein in Yellowknife Bay, the mission's first sample drilling on Mars.

PIA17595, a Curiosity mosaic showing the stacked geological members of the Yellowknife Bay formation and marking the two places where the rover drilled into the lowest member, Sheepbed, at the targets John Klein and Cumberland.

PIA20334, a Mars Hand Lens Imager view of Curiosity's left middle and left rear wheels, part of a routine wheel inspection set taken on 18 April 2016, sol 1315, showing punctures and tears in the aluminium skin.

PIA19142, a Curiosity self-portrait at the Mojave site on lower Aeolis Mons, combining dozens of Mars Hand Lens Imager frames taken on sols 868, 882 and 884 in January 2015, where the drill collected the mission's second sample of the mountain.

A digital render of a white conical capsule carrying a small Mars One roundel, hanging above a rocky red plain on its descent engines with its landing legs out and a dust cloud rolling away downrange; on the Mars One roadmap page this illustrated the 2016 supply mission, which the accompanying text said would launch in January 2016 and land that October with 2,500 kilograms of spares, solar panels and supplies.
credit: Mars One Foundation; the concept art on the Mars One website is attributed to Bryan Versteeg of spacehabs.com, who English Wikipedia records created all the animations and illustrations used on it. Mars One published the images without a per-image credit line, so the attribution rests on that secondary record rather than on the file itself.

caption: A digital render of a low six-wheeled rover with a flat solar deck and a mast, driving across a rock-strewn red plain in low, raking light that throws long shadows; the Mars One roadmap text beside it described a 2018 settlement rover whose job was to find the exact site for the outpost and stream video to Earth continuously.
credit: Mars One Foundation; the concept art on the Mars One website is attributed to Bryan Versteeg of spacehabs.com, who English Wikipedia records created all the animations and illustrations used on it. Mars One published the images without a per-image credit line, so the attribution rests on that secondary record rather than on the file itself.

caption: A digital render of six identical white conical landers standing in a row on a red plain with two rovers moving between them and dark solar panels laid out on the ground; the Mars One roadmap text for 2021 described exactly this, two living units, two life support units, a second supply unit and another rover arriving in six separate landers to be assembled before any crew left Earth.
credit: Mars One Foundation; the concept art on the Mars One website is attributed to Bryan Versteeg of spacehabs.com, who English Wikipedia records created all the animations and illustrations used on it. Mars One published the images without a per-image credit line, so the attribution rests on that secondary record rather than on the file itself.

caption: A digital render of the grown settlement, a dozen white conical capsules joined by low inflatable tunnels buried under mounded regolith, with fields of solar panels in the foreground, a rover, a suited figure walking between the capsules and hills on the horizon; on the roadmap this illustrated 2025, when a second crew of four was to land and be met by the first.
credit: Mars One Foundation; the concept art on the Mars One website is attributed to Bryan Versteeg of spacehabs.com, who English Wikipedia records created all the animations and illustrations used on it. Mars One published the images without a per-image credit line, so the attribution rests on that secondary record rather than on the file itself.

caption: A portrait of Bas Lansdorp, the Dutch engineer who co-founded Mars One and was its chief executive, standing beneath a large refracting telescope in an observatory dome. Campus Party Brasil published it on 29 January 2015 in its set of keynote speakers and highlights for CPBR8; that event ran from 3 to 7 February 2015, so the frame was issued ahead of the conference rather than shot on its floor.
credit: Campus Party Brasil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

caption: The foundation's own early artist's conception of the Inspiration Mars vehicle: a crew capsule on a cylindrical service module with two dark solar arrays, docked nose to nose with a ribbed white inflatable habitat lettered InspirationMARS, coasting above the orange limb of the planet.
credit: Inspiration Mars Foundation, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

caption: A diagram issued by the Inspiration Mars Foundation showing the flyby geometry at closest approach: a globe of Mars with its north polar cap, a heavy arrow labelled Towards Sun pointing away to the upper left, a yellow line marking the terminator, and the spacecraft's path drawn as a curve down the right-hand side with a dot at periapsis and a dashed section where it passes into shadow.
credit: Inspiration Mars Foundation, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

caption: A schematic of the free-return loop, drawn by a Wikimedia contributor from a Space.com infographic and labelled not to scale, showing the Sun at centre with the dotted orbits of Venus, Earth and Mars, and the spacecraft track marked Earth launch 5 January 2018, 228 days outbound, Mars fly-by 21 August 2018, 273 days inbound and Earth return 21 May 2019.
credit: Cmglee, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

caption: A NASA photograph of Dennis Tito speaking at the 40th Space Congress in Cape Canaveral on 30 April 2003, two years after he became the first private citizen to visit the International Space Station and ten years before he announced Inspiration Mars.

True-colour view of the whole Martian disc built from Mars Colour Camera frames taken on 10 October 2014 from about 76,000 km, showing the Tharsis volcanoes and Valles Marineris, processed by Justin Cowart from ISRO's archived data.
credit: ISRO / ISSDC / Justin Cowart, CC BY 2.0

caption: The Mars Orbiter Mission spacecraft in an ISRO cleanroom during assembly in October 2013, with its high-gain antenna, solar array and 440 N liquid apogee motor visible.
ISRO engineers loading the Mars Orbiter Mission spacecraft into the Large Space Simulation Chamber at ISAC in Bengaluru for thermal vacuum testing before launch.
PSLV-C25 lifting off from the First Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota, at 09:08 UTC on 5 November 2013, carrying the Mars Orbiter Mission.
credit: ISRO / Government of India, Press Information Bureau photo 50447 (GODL-India)

caption: The ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network control room in Bengaluru on the morning of 24 September 2014, as Mars orbit insertion is confirmed, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi present.
credit: Prime Minister's Office, Government of India (GODL-India)

caption: India photographed by the Mars Colour Camera on 19 November 2013 from about 70,000 km, the first Earth image returned by the mission, taken while the spacecraft was still in its highly elliptical Earth orbit awaiting trans-Mars injection. Released by ISRO in its Mars Colour Camera gallery.
Engineers and technicians test deploy MAVEN's twin solar arrays inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center on 23 September 2013, about eight weeks before launch.
The United Launch Alliance Atlas V carrying MAVEN lifts off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral on 18 November 2013.

False colour ultraviolet images of Mars in three wavelength bands, taken by MAVEN's Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrograph from an altitude of 36,500 km eight hours after orbit insertion in September 2014. Blue shows sunlight scattered by the extended cloud of atomic hydrogen escaping the planet.

The assembled ExoMars 2016 spacecraft composite, the Trace Gas Orbiter with the Schiaparelli demonstrator mounted on it, photographed on 2 March 2016 at the Baikonur cosmodrome as the second half of the Proton launcher fairing is lowered around it by overhead crane.

The 1.194 m diameter, 3.5 m high composite central cylinder that carries launch loads through the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter and houses its propellant and oxidiser tanks, seen during integration of the spacecraft's electrical subsystems in the Thales Alenia Space cleanroom at Cannes, France.

Frost-fringed polygonal ground on a springtime morning in the southern mid-latitudes of Mars near Dorsa Brevia, captured on 21 June 2020 by the CaSSIS colour and stereo camera on the Trace Gas Orbiter.

HiRISE view taken on 25 October 2016, six days after the crash, of the ground in Meridiani Planum where Schiaparelli came down, with magnified insets of three places where parts of the spacecraft reached the surface: the lander module's dark impact scar, the parachute with the back shell, and the front heat shield.
The Schiaparelli entry, descent and landing demonstrator being unpacked in a cleanroom at the Baikonur cosmodrome in January 2016, before being mated to the Trace Gas Orbiter for launch.

The first colour HiRISE view of the Schiaparelli impact site, observed on 1 November 2016, presented as three cutouts: the lander module at top, the parachute and back shell at lower left, and the heat shield at lower right, which fell outside the colour strip and so appears without colour.

InSight's first full selfie, a mosaic of 11 frames taken by the Instrument Deployment Camera on the elbow of the robotic arm on 6 December 2018, showing the solar panels, the deck, the weather sensor booms and the UHF antenna.
The Atlas V 401 carrying InSight and the two MarCO CubeSats climbing into thick fog from Space Launch Complex 3 at Vandenberg Air Force Base before dawn on 5 May 2018.
The copper-coloured SEIS seismometer standing on the Martian surface near dusk on 19 December 2018, photographed by the camera on InSight's robotic arm shortly after the arm set it down.
The dome-shaped Wind and Thermal Shield in place over the seismometer after InSight lowered it on 2 February 2019, sol 66.
The pit around the HP3 mole as it looked after hammering on 9 January 2021, sol 754, with the scoop on the robotic arm above it and the copper science tether running away to the left.
InSight's final selfie, a mosaic assembled from images taken on 24 April 2022, sol 1211, with the solar panels and deck buried under a thick coat of Martian dust.
One of the last images InSight returned, taken on 11 December 2022, sol 1436, showing the seismometer under its shield on the ground in front of the lander.

Engineer Joel Steinkraus with both MarCO spacecraft at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in March 2018. The unit on the left is folded as it flew stowed on the rocket; the one on the right has its solar panels out, with its flat reflectarray high-gain antenna standing up behind it.

Mars photographed by MarCO-B's wide-angle camera on 26 November 2018 as the CubeSat flew away after InSight landed, with the grid of its reflectarray antenna along the right edge of the frame. The picture sits letterboxed inside a 1920 by 1080 canvas.

NASA's annotated version of MarCO-B's wide-angle camera view, taken as a test of exposure settings on 2 October 2018. Mars is the small red dot right of centre, ringed with a dashed circle and labelled by NASA; parts of the CubeSat's unfolded high-gain antenna show on both sides of the frame.
The first image returned by MarCO-B after launch, showing its unfolded high-gain antenna at right and Earth with the Moon as two points of light near the centre.

The Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package standing on a bench in a cleanroom in Germany before launch, released by JPL as PIA23044 with the caption that the heat probe was being tested in Germany. JPL does not state whether the unit shown is the flight model. The black upright tube is the support structure that holds the mole; the horizontal box beside it carries the tether compartments, and a separate electronics box sits on a cloth at the right. Yellow ESD tape reading ESD GESCHÜTZTER BEREICH runs across the foreground.

A labelled rendering of the whole HP3 instrument, published by JPL under the title HP3 Cutaway Rendering (Artist's Concept). It annotates the grapple point, the tether length monitor, the tether compartments, the engineering tether, the feet, the connectors box, the orange science tether embedded with passive temperature sensors, and the mole itself, described as carrying the hammering mechanism, heaters and sensors for thermal conductivity, and static tilt sensors.

A frame from InSight's Instrument Deployment Camera showing the HP3 support structure standing on the ground of Elysium Planitia with the robotic arm's grapple directly above it and the engineering tether looping back towards the lander. JPL's caption states that InSight set the heat probe on the Martian surface on 12 February 2019.

An Instrument Deployment Camera frame from 26 October 2019, Sol 325, published by JPL with the caption that the mole is seen after backing about halfway out of the hole it had burrowed. The pale mole body lies tilted at upper left, half out of the ground, with the dark scoop of the robotic arm set into the pit beside it and the science tether running off to the left.

An Instrument Deployment Camera frame from 20 June 2020 showing the scoop on the end of InSight's robotic arm pressed down into the mole's pit, holding the mole in the ground. JPL's caption records that the movement of sand grains inside the scoop suggested the mole was bumping up against the bottom of the scoop while hammering.

An Instrument Deployment Camera frame from 9 January 2021, Sol 754, published by JPL as the mole after its final hammering session. The scoop is pressed into the loose regolith that had been scraped over the buried mole, the science tether runs away to the left, and the disturbed ground of the pit is visible around it. JPL's caption states that with no progress the team called an end to their efforts that day.

Rosetta photographed by the CIVA camera on its own Philae lander four minutes before closest approach on 25 February 2007, from about 1,000 km, showing one of the 14 m solar wings and part of the spacecraft body against the northern hemisphere of Mars around Mawrth Vallis. ESA's caption states that the frame was taken in black and white, that representative colour was added to the Martian surface for the 2007 release, and that the colours were slightly enhanced again for this 2014 version.

A four-panel comparison released on 4 June 2009, pairing strips of Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera mosaic with the same ground as recorded by Dawn's framing camera during the gravity assist of 17 February 2009, and then laying the Dawn frames over the HRSC mosaic. The Dawn images were taken to check the camera's performance rather than to do Mars science.

A colourised composite of thermal frames taken by the E-THEMIS instrument on NASA's Europa Clipper during its Mars gravity assist on 1 March 2025, when the imager shot one picture per second for about 18 minutes. NASA's release gives red as ground near 0 degrees Celsius and purple as about minus 125 degrees Celsius. The frames were greyscale and were taken to calibrate the instrument for Europa; the colour is applied to infrared brightness rather than to anything the eye could see.

An ESA infographic published on 10 March 2025 setting out Hera's Mars swingby in four numbered steps: first sighting of Mars about ten days out when the planet is ten pixels across, closest approach at around 5,000 km from the surface and 300 km from Deimos, a chance at Phobos on departure, and the note that Hera's speed relative to Mars is unchanged while its direction is not. A panel at the bottom credits ESOC flight dynamics and the SPICE visualisation team at ESAC.

Mars as a thin crescent, acquired with Imager A of Psyche's multispectral imager at about 5:03 a.m. PDT on 15 May 2026 as the spacecraft closed on the planet for its gravity assist, and processed into a natural colour view from red, green and blue filter data. NASA describes it as the last view of the whole planet before Mars overfilled the camera's field, and notes the crescent was brighter and reached farther around the disc than predicted because of sunlight scattering through the dusty atmosphere.

An enhanced-colour mosaic of four multispectral imager frames taken on 15 May 2026 during Psyche's Mars flyby, covering the southern highlands of Iapygia between roughly 62 and 78 degrees east longitude and 4 degrees north to 14 degrees south latitude. Fournier crater, about 114 km (71 miles) across, sits below centre, and the linear scarps of Oenotria Scopuli, part of the Isidis basin structure, run down the frame. A 100 km scale bar and a north arrow are printed at the top right.

A composite of two of the best HiRISE frames of comet C/2013 A1 Siding Spring, taken from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter on 19 October 2014 at the minimum distance of 138,000 km and a scale of 138 metres per pixel. The top row shows the full dynamic range, with the nucleus and the bright inner coma; the bottom row is stretched to bring out the fainter outer coma and saturates the middle. Only two to three pixels cross the brightest feature, which implies a nucleus smaller than 0.5 km.

A plotted spectrum with no picture of the sky in it. It shows the Martian ultraviolet spectrum measured by MAVEN's Imaging Ultraviolet Spectrograph before and after the Siding Spring meteor shower of 19 October 2014, with a blue trace for the quiet atmosphere and a red trace for the aftermath. Where the red rises above the blue, metals from comet dust have been added; the tall spike near 280 nanometres is ionised magnesium. Released on 7 November 2014.

Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS as HiRISE recorded it on 2 October 2025, when the comet was about 0.2 astronomical units, roughly 29.9 million km, from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. The HiRISE team gives a 3.2 second exposure at a scale of 30 km per pixel, notes that the nucleus cannot be resolved and that spacecraft jitter smears the object across several pixels, and says the full coma spans the whole frame while only the brightest inner part registers.

Comet 3I/ATLAS as the Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System on ESA's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter saw it on 3 October 2025 from 30 million km, a slightly fuzzy dot towards the right of a field of trailed stars. ESA states that the detection needed multiple five-second exposures stacked, on an instrument built to photograph the bright surface of Mars a few hundred to a few thousand kilometres below.

3I/ATLAS photographed by the high-resolution camera on the Tianwen-1 orbiter, published by CNSA on 6 November 2025. The caption under the image on the CNSA release reads 天问一号环绕器高分辨率相机拍摄到的阿特拉斯（成像时间10月3日，成像距离约2896万千米）, giving an imaging date of 3 October and an imaging distance of about 28.96 million km. The comet appears as a small bright smudge of nucleus and coma in a field of stars; CNSA says the data were received and processed by the ground application system.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration), 天问一号环绕器高分辨率相机

caption: A composite of seven Mastcam-Z frames from NASA's Perseverance rover showing Earth as a small bright dot moving from upper left to lower right and passing behind the Martian moon Phobos on 2 July 2026, sol 1907 of the mission. Earth was about 314 million km away and one pixel wide; Phobos, roughly 27 km across at its widest, appears about a third the width of the Moon seen from Earth.

Opportunity's view of the fading Martian twilight about an hour after sunset on its 449th sol, 29 April 2005, as the stars were coming out. The pale dot near the centre of this narrow published crop is not a star but Earth. NASA's caption for the release notes the exposure was long enough that the planet's motion elongated it.

The Kazachok landing platform in the clean room at Thales Alenia Space in Turin in November 2020, sitting on a supporting trolley with its ramps and solar panels folded, while the dark rear jacket of the descent module hangs from a red lifting frame directly above it and engineers work at floor level. ESA's caption records that the front shield would later be fitted to the same trolley, and that the platform and the Rosalind Franklin rover would then undergo joint testing at Cannes.
credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

caption: The Rosalind Franklin rover in its stowed configuration sitting on top of the Kazachok surface platform in a clean room at Thales Alenia Space in Cannes, two of the platform's ramps deployed down to the floor on either side and one of its solar panels partially deployed at the front left, the platform itself standing on a wheeled support trolley rather than on its own landing legs. ESA's caption records that the two were mated to form the landing module and that the tests included electrical, power and data transfer checks between them.
credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

caption: The Russian landing platform suspended from a hoist as it is unpacked in Turin in March 2019, its white upper panels and the dark frame of its ramps visible, with a technician in a clean-room suit steadying it. ESA's caption records that the platform left Russia in March 2019 packed to planetary protection requirements, flew to Turin on an Antonov with its ground support equipment, and that Roscosmos announced its new name, Kazachok, at this point.
credit: Thales Alenia Space (credit line given on the ESA image page)

caption: A Lavochkin computer drawing of the landing platform from above and from below, labelled in Russian for марсоход (the rover), трапы (the ramps), панели СБ (the solar panels), служебная и научная аппаратура (the service and science equipment), баки с топливом (the propellant tanks) and посадочные опоры (the landing legs).

A Lavochkin diagram of the entry, descent and landing sequence drawn over a Martian horizon and keyed in Russian with times, altitudes and speeds: entry at t equals 0 at 120 km and 6.1 km/s, peak heating, first stage of the parachute system, main parachute, front shield separation, separation of the rear cover with the parachute, end of braking, engine cut-off and touchdown at about 1.2 to 1.45 m/s, then the landing platform deploying its solar panels and ramps.

NASA's artist illustration of the International Mars Ice Mapper, published with the 3 February 2021 announcement of the statement of intent. The radar orbiter is in the foreground low over Mars with its solar wings out and a large mesh reflector carried above it on a boom, a wedge shaped radar swath cutting down into the ground below it, and three smaller relay orbiters strung out higher up with a beam running to Earth at the top right. NASA's own file metadata captions it as four orbiters that are part of the I-MIM mission.

JAXA's own chart of its Strategic Mars Exploration Program, published with its 3 March 2021 statement on the Mars Ice Mapper agreement. A grey arrow curves from the 2020s at the lower left, through Martian Moons Exploration and its objectives, up through a Small Orbiter and EDL Demonstration box captioned Distribution and Inventory of Water with an inset picture of MIM beside it, on to lander and rover exploration in the 2030s captioned Evolution of Water, and finally to multiple and sustainable Mars exploration at 20xx.

A global map of buried water ice on Mars released by JPL on 10 December 2019, made by combining data from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey and Mars Global Surveyor. Colour gives the depth to ice over a grey shaded relief base, from magenta at less than about 10 cm to red at more than 80 cm; the black areas are ground where a landing spacecraft would sink into fine dust, and the white outlined box in the northern mid latitudes marks the region JPL calls ideal for sending astronauts who need to dig up water ice.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: A four-wheeled Sample Fetch Rover development vehicle, nicknamed Codi and carrying Airbus and ESA markings on its wheel bogies, standing on bare excavated ground with spoil heaps behind it during ESA and Airbus field trials at Stevenage in the United Kingdom in mid-October 2023. Its blue robotic arm is extended down and forward toward a sample tube lying on the ground at the left, and a camera head and mast rise above the open tubular chassis. GMV records that the rover drove about 300 metres around obstacles and then detected and collected the tube with no human intervention, and that ESA continued the Airbus-led project after the fetch rover had been removed from Mars Sample Return.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: ESA's 2019 infographic of the Mars Sample Return architecture, drawn as one continuous white line from Earth to Mars and back. Three rockets stand on Earth at the bottom, labelled Mars 2020 mission, Sample Retrieval Lander mission and Earth Return Orbiter mission. On the Martian surface the NASA rover leaves red sample canisters, a small blue ESA rover drives out to collect them and returns them to the lander, and a rocket carries the container up to orbit, where the orbiter captures it, sheds its modules and drops a capsule onto the Earth.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: A NASA illustration released on 21 April 2022 showing the Sample Retrieval Lander on the Martian surface with the Mars Ascent Vehicle climbing away from it on a bright plume, the sample container inside the rocket's white nose cone. The lander stands on legs with a ring of petal-shaped solar arrays spread around it and four spherical gold-wrapped tanks on the deck. NASA's caption gives the rocket a height of about 3 metres and describes a robotic arm loading Perseverance's sealed tubes into the nose cone before launch.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: A frame from a camera inside JPL's 25-Foot Space Simulator, burned in with the timestamp 2023-09-15 18:13:13, showing the dual rotor system for the next generation of Mars helicopters mounted on a steel test rig against the chamber's black corrugated wall, with a white baffle hung behind the blades. NASA's caption records that over three weeks the carbon fibre blades, longer and stronger than those on the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, were spun at ever higher speeds and greater pitch angles and reached Mach 0.95 at the tips.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: An artist's concept of ESA's Earth Return Orbiter above Mars, showing a compact body carrying a dish antenna and a payload stack, with two very long solar wings of many rectangular panels spread either side of it. The cratered limb of Mars fills the lower part of the frame, and a yellow disc on the limb at the left edge is one of a chain of lens flares thrown by the sun off frame to the right, and should not be mistaken for a moon. NASA's caption describes the spacecraft that would have been the largest ever to orbit Mars and the first interplanetary spacecraft to capture samples in orbit and make a return trip between Earth and Mars.

mission_name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
caption: A photograph taken at Airbus in July 2025 during integration of the oxidiser tank into the Earth Return Orbiter's Orbit Insertion Module. The module's flight structure, its black and foil-wrapped central tube braced by blue handling beams, hangs from an overhead crane on a lifting frame above a foil-covered tank standing on a trolley; two technicians in cleanroom coveralls work at the interface ring, one of them in an Airbus suit and orange helmet with his back to the camera, and a placard on the handling frame reads ASSEMBLY WEIGHT 1050 KG. ESA's caption for the frame reads Oxidiser tank integration into the Orbit Insertion Module.

The image CNSA publishes as “着巡合影”图, the lander and rover group photo, shot from ground level with the Zhurong rover at the left, solar wings and mast deployed and a red flag on its body, and the landing platform at the right. CNSA's own text states that the rover drove to about 10 m south of the landing platform, released the separation camera mounted on its underside, reversed back towards the platform, and that the camera photographed the rover moving and then the rover and platform together, the frames going by radio to the rover and on to Earth through the orbiter relay.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

caption: The Tianwen-1 cruise stack against empty black space, the white entry capsule at the top, the gold-blanketed orbiter below it with the red Chinese flag on its side, the high-gain dish at the left and a solar wing at the right. CNSA released it on 1 October 2020 and states that the flight image was taken by a 分离测量传感器, a separation measurement sensor, mounted on the outside of the spacecraft and released from it under ground control, using two wide-angle lenses to take one image a second and returning them over a WiFi link.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

caption: The whole Tianwen-1 orbiter seen from outside, flying above the white north polar cap of Mars with its gold body, silver directional antenna, solar wings and radar antenna deployed. CNSA published it in its New Year release of 1 January 2022, identifying the dark region below as Olympia Undae and the bright crater at upper left as Korolev, and describing the polar ice as a mixture of dry ice and water ice. The release describes the scene in detail but does not say how the picture was taken.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

caption: A close view along the flank of the Tianwen-1 orbiter, the gold thermal blanketing and the high-gain dish filling the right of the frame, one solar wing fully deployed at the left, a subsurface radar antenna running parallel to it and the magnetometer boom extending, in CNSA's words, towards the orbiter's upper left, with Mars filling the background. CNSA publishes it in the same 1 January 2022 release as 环绕器局部特写, a close-up of part of the orbiter.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

caption: The image CNSA publishes as “中国印迹”图, China's imprint, showing the Zhurong landing platform alone on the surface with the Chinese flag on its side, its ramps lowered and the rover's wheel tracks curving away across the ground to the right. CNSA's text states it was taken by the rover from about 6 m away in the direction 东偏南 60°, east rotated 60 degrees towards south, so it came from the rover itself and not from the dropped separation camera. CNSA does not name which of the rover's cameras took it.
credit: 国家航天局 (China National Space Administration)

caption: Hope's first science image of Mars, taken by the Emirates eXploration Imager on 10 February 2021 from about 24,700 km altitude, one day after orbit insertion, showing the north polar region and Olympus Mons catching the sunrise.
The full disc of Mars assembled from Hope EXI red, green and blue filter frames taken on 1 May 2021 during orbit 47, from a spacecraft altitude of 21,519 km, processed by Andrea Luck.

A labelled composite graphic titled 'The Ultraviolet Colors of the Red Planet', showing four false-colour ultraviolet views of Mars from the Emirates Mars Ultraviolet Spectrometer, grouped by species: hydrogen at 102.6 and 121.6 nm, oxygen at 130.4 nm and the 135.6 nm oxygen glow driven by energetic electrons, and carbon monoxide emission between 140 and 160 nm. The instrument team assembled the labelled graphic out of spectrometer data, so no single camera frame looks like this.

Omran Sharaf, project manager of the Emirates Mars Mission, speaking at the official announcement of the mission's scientific objectives at Al Bahr Palace in Dubai on 6 May 2015, in front of Arabic text reading 'First Arab probe to explore Mars'.

The sealed shipping container carrying the Hope spacecraft being lifted from a Volga-Dnepr Antonov freighter in Japan in late April 2020, after the flight from Dubai. The spacecraft itself is inside the container and not visible; the container carries the mission decal.
A full-size mockup of the Hope orbiter displayed at the International Astronautical Congress in Dubai in October 2021, showing the hexagonal bus, the two solar wings and the high-gain antenna.

PIA24550, a Mastcam-Z mosaic taken on 19 April 2021 after Ingenuity's first flight, showing the helicopter standing on its four legs on the floor of Jezero crater at Wright Brothers Field, with rover wheel tracks crossing the foreground.

PIA24584, the image Ingenuity's downward-looking black-and-white navigation camera took of its own shadow while hovering above Jezero crater on 19 April 2021, during the first instance of powered, controlled flight on another planet.
PIA24648, a Mastcam-Z view of Ingenuity standing at its new landing site after Flight 5 on 7 May 2021, a one-way trip of 129 m to a height record of 10 m that lasted 108 seconds.

PIA26243, a colour image from Ingenuity's horizon-facing camera showing the shadow of one of its rotor blades cast on the sand after Flight 72 on 18 January 2024, with a clear step in the silhouette where the outer part of the blade is missing.

PIA26236, an enhanced-colour mosaic of six Mastcam-Z frames taken on 4 February 2024 from about 450 m away, showing Ingenuity where it came to rest at the spot the team named Valinor Hills after its 72nd and last flight.

PIA26482, a NASA graphic published in December 2024 depicting the most likely sequence for Ingenuity's hard landing on Flight 72: high horizontal velocity at touchdown on a sloping sand ripple, causing the helicopter to pitch and roll and the blades to fail.
PIA24597, members of the Ingenuity team in the control room at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory reacting to the data showing the helicopter had completed its second flight on Mars, on 22 April 2021.

A six kopeck Soviet stamp issued in 1972 and headed Автоматическая станция «Марс-2»: вымпел на планете 27.11.71 г., showing a painted M-71 station firing its engine beside a crescent Mars, with an inset panel at the upper left depicting the pennant itself: a plate carrying the State Emblem of the USSR and the words ЗЕМЛЯ МАРС СССР 1971.
credit: Почта СССР (USSR Post); scan by Andrew Butko, via Wikimedia Commons

caption: A Spirit navigation camera view of the aluminium memorial plaque bolted to the back of the rover's high-gain antenna, reading IN MEMORIAM, TO THE CREW OF THE SPACE SHUTTLE COLUMBIA, STS-107, FEBRUARY 1, 2003, with the seven crew names, a shuttle silhouette, a United States flag and the NASA insignia, photographed on the surface of Gusev crater.

A framed pair of documents held by the National Air and Space Museum: on the left the 18 May 1984 instrument signed by Walter J. Boyne and NASA Administrator James M. Beggs transferring the Mutch Memorial Station, meaning Viking Lander 1 on Mars, to the museum and charging it to retain, secure and protect the plaque until astronauts can affix it; on the right the Thomas A. Mutch Memorial Station plaque itself, signed by Administrator Robert A. Frosch on 7 January 1981 and carrying the dedication to the memory of Tim Mutch, with a blank line at the foot reading Emplaced.
credit: Mark Avino, Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum (NASM2026-01015)

caption: Two panoramic camera views of the MarsDial on Spirit's solar deck, taken on Mars near local noon and again later in the afternoon so the shadow of the central post falls differently, with the colour and grey calibration blocks at the corners and the ring of text around the dial.

The primary Mastcam-Z calibration target for the Perseverance rover photographed on Earth before launch, showing the black shadow post at the centre, the grey and colour swatches, and around the rim a fern, an Apatosaurus, a man and a woman raising their hands in greeting, a rocket running from a blue dot to a red dot, a model of the inner solar system, a DNA helix, cyanobacteria and the motto TWO WORLDS, ONE BEGINNING.

A photograph of Perseverance's supersonic parachute taken by an up-look camera on the backshell during the descent to Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, with NASA's annotation overlaid showing how the orange and white gores encode DARE MIGHTY THINGS in binary across the inner rings and the coordinates of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory around the outer band.

PIA26344, a Perseverance self-portrait made from 62 WATSON frames taken on 23 July 2024, with the arrowhead-shaped rock nicknamed Cheyava Falls lying to the left of the rover near the centre of the picture.

PIA24428, a still frame from video shot by a downward-looking camera on the descent stage as Perseverance was lowered on the sky crane's cables toward the floor of Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, with dust raised by the descent engines around the rover.

The United Launch Alliance Atlas V 541 lifting off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station on 30 July 2020 at 7:50 a.m. EDT, carrying Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter, seen from the Atlas Space Operations Center.

PIA25212, a Mastcam-Z panorama of 64 frames taken on 11 April 2022, sol 406, looking out across the fan-shaped river delta on the western side of Jezero crater, with sand bedforms running along its base. NASA states that the colour bands have been processed to accentuate differences and that the sky would not look blue to a human standing there.

PIA24203, the gold-plated Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment photographed after installation inside Perseverance's body before launch, with the wide intake tube for filtered Martian carbon dioxide on its top surface.

PIA24832, a Mastcam-Z image taken on 4 September 2021 looking into the drill to confirm that a rock core had been retained inside the sample tube held there, the core later sealed as the sample Montdenier.
PIA23268, engineers and technicians installing the remote sensing mast on the Mars 2020 rover in High Bay 1 of the Spacecraft Assembly Facility at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory on 5 June 2019.

A close-up of a gloved hand holding the small mounted silicon chip that carries about 35,000 laser-engraved signatures collected from visitors to the Mars Exploration Rovers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, photographed before the chip was fitted to the second rover.
The dime-sized mounted microchip carrying 826,923 names submitted by the public, held in a gloved hand in the clean room where the InSight lander was built, before it was affixed to the lander deck.

The anodised placard installed on the aft crossbeam of the Perseverance rover on 16 March 2020, etched with Earth and Mars joined by rays from the Sun, with three fingernail-sized silicon chips fixed in the upper left corner and a leader line labelling them 10,932,295 Explorers.

A close-up of the silica glass DVD on Opportunity's lander, made by the Student Astronauts from three Pancam frames taken through different filters on sol 2, showing the LEGO astrobot figure at the centre, the dust-collecting magnets and the ring of black dashes around the rim that encodes a hidden message.
credit: NASA / JPL-Caltech / Cornell / The Planetary Society; composite by the Student Astronauts

caption: A twenty frame panoramic camera mosaic that Spirit took of its own empty lander, the Columbia Memorial Station, after driving off it on sol 16 in January 2004, showing the open petals, the deflated airbags and the JPL markings. The Planetary Society's caption for the same mosaic notes that the Red Rover Goes to Mars DVD is visible toward the back of the right-hand petal.

A press photograph of the Mars Microphone held flat on an open hand, showing the gold-framed board with its ceramic processor package, the two small can-shaped components, a second gold-lidded chip and a rainbow ribbon cable running off the edge. The Planetary Society captions it as the flight spare of the Society's Mars Microphone, the twin of the unit that flew aboard Mars Polar Lander.
credit: © Robin Weiner, Associated Press, via The Planetary Society

caption: A studio photograph of a Phoenix Mars Descent Imager, its housing marked MARDI 3, lying on a white surface with a pocket knife beside it for scale and a harness of ribbon cable running out of the back. A white leader line labelled microphone points to the small capsule mounted on the side of the camera body. Malin Space Science Systems publishes the frame on its Phoenix MARDI page labelled only Phoenix Mars Descent Imager with microphone, with no date, so whether this is the flight unit or a spare is not stated.

A cleanroom photograph of the SuperCam mast unit on Perseverance's remote sensing mast, with a black leader line labelled Microphone pointing to the small cylindrical fitting on the left flank of the white housing, next to the telescope aperture. The Mastcam-Z cameras and the navigation cameras are visible below.

A cleanroom photograph of the port side of Perseverance during assembly at JPL, with a black leader line labelled Microphone pointing to the grey box mounted on top of a black cable bracket amid bundles of gold-taped harness. JPL's caption notes this microphone was provided to record entry, descent and landing, and that it did not do so.

The Tianwen-1 orbiter photographed in Mars orbit by a small camera the spacecraft released, showing the gold-foiled bus, both solar wings, the high-gain antenna and the subsurface radar booms, with Mars filling the frame behind it and the bright north polar cap at upper left.
credit: CNSA / China Planetary Exploration Program; via Ling Xin, National Science Review (article CC BY 4.0)

caption: A Long March 5 Y4 rocket lifting off from Launch Complex 101 at the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan at 04:41:15 UT on 23 July 2020, carrying the five-tonne Tianwen-1 stack.
credit: 中新网 (China News Service), CC BY 4.0

caption: HiRISE image of the Tianwen-1 landing site in southern Utopia Planitia acquired on 6 June 2021, showing the landing platform surrounded by the bright blast pattern of its descent engines and the Zhurong rover a short distance to the south.

China's first global colour image map of Mars, at 76 metres per pixel, assembled from Tianwen-1 Moderate Resolution Imaging Camera coverage and shown here in Robinson projection with a graticule and scale bar.
credit: Jianjun Liu, Xin Ren, Wei Yan et al., Science Bulletin, CC BY 4.0; data CNSA / Tianwen-1 Ground Research and Application System

caption: Olympus Mons under water-ice cloud, made from seven Tianwen-1 Moderate Resolution Imaging Camera frames taken on 30 December 2021 from 627 km altitude, mosaicked and reprojected by Andrea Luck from data released through moon.bao.ac.cn.
credit: Raw image CNSA/CLEP/PEC/MoRIC; image processing Andrea Luck, CC BY 2.0

caption: The Tianwen-1 landing platform standing on its four legs in southern Utopia Planitia with its deployment ramp lowered and the Chinese flag on its side, photographed by the Zhurong rover after it drove off on 22 May 2021.
credit: CNSA / China Planetary Exploration Program; via Huang, X., Xu, C., Hu, J. et al., Astrodynamics (article CC BY 4.0)

caption: A labelled engineering diagram of the Tianwen-1 orbiter, drawn from the CAD model and shown from two angles, marking where its science instruments sit: the high- and medium-resolution cameras (HiRIC, MoRIC), the subsurface radar (MOSIR), the mineralogy spectrometer (MMS), the magnetometer (MOMAG) and the particle analysers (MINPA, MEPA).
credit: Li, C., Zhang, R., Yu, D. et al., Space Science Reviews, CC BY 4.0

caption: Zhurong and the Tianwen-1 landing platform standing side by side on the surface of southern Utopia Planitia, photographed by a small wireless camera that the rover set down on the ground and then drove away from.
credit: 中国新闻网 (China News Service), CC BY 4.0; original imagery CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program

caption: A crop of the deployable-camera portrait showing the Zhurong rover alone: the butterfly-wing solar arrays, the mast with the navigation and terrain cameras, the directional antenna and the six wheels.
credit: 中国新闻网 (China News Service), CC BY 4.0; original imagery CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program

caption: A colour panorama of southern Utopia Planitia from Zhurong, showing bright wind-shaped sand ridges running across a rock-strewn plain to a flat horizon, with part of the rover's own hardware in the lower left of the frame.
credit: He Zhu, National Science Review, CC BY 4.0; imagery CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program (Zhurong)

caption: A wide-angle hazard-avoidance camera view from Zhurong showing two lines of wheel tracks running back across the plain, with a red box drawn at upper left around the discarded backshell and parachute of the entry capsule.
credit: CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program (Zhurong hazard-avoidance camera). No individual photographer; the frame is camera-generated.

caption: HiRISE image of southern Utopia Planitia acquired on 11 March 2022 in which the Zhurong rover's entire southward traverse of roughly 1.5 km can be traced as a pair of wheel tracks on the surface.

PIA24914, a HiRISE view of Utopia Planitia acquired on 1 August 2021 and projected at 25 centimetres per pixel, showing the flat plain south of the landing site with impact craters, light-toned wind-blown ridges and troughs.
A HiRISE cutout from 6 June 2021 showing the discarded heat shield of the Tianwen-1 entry capsule lying on the surface of southern Utopia Planitia, with the dark impact mark it made on landing.

PIA25738, a photomontage of ten WATSON images, each showing one sealed titanium sample tube lying on the Martian surface shortly after Perseverance set it down at Three Forks between 21 December 2022 and 28 January 2023. From the left: Malay, Mageik, Crosswind Lake, Roubion, Coulettes, Montdenier, Bearwallow, Skyland, Atsah and Amalik.

PIA25340, the WATSON camera on Perseverance's robotic arm photographing the tenth and final tube of the Three Forks depot on the ground on 28 January 2023, sol 690. It is the witness tube sealed at the Amalik sampling site, the only witness tube placed in the depot.

PIA25736, Perseverance's Mastcam-Z portrait of the finished sample depot taken on 31 January 2023, sol 693, stitched from 368 individual frames, with the colour adjusted to approximate what the surface would look like to the human eye. The full photojournal original is 29705 by 20033 pixels and about 77 MB; this is NASA's own smaller rendition of the same image.

PIA25682, NASA's map of the Three Forks depot, with a labelled circle marking where each of the ten tubes was deployed in the zigzag pattern, the tubes set roughly 5 to 15 m apart so a recovery vehicle could reach them safely.
PIA25663, a composite of stitched WATSON frames showing the first sample tube Perseverance deposited on the Martian surface on 21 December 2022, sol 653, the igneous core informally named Malay.

Deimos as a dark, irregular silhouette against the brighter disc of Mars, in a monochrome visible-light frame from Hera's 1020 by 1020 pixel Asteroid Framing Camera taken during the gravity assist of 12 March 2025 from about 1,000 km. ESA's caption places the bright Terra Sabaea region at the top, part of the 450 km Huygens crater at the right and part of Hellas Basin at the bottom right.

The same encounter in mid-infrared, from the Thermal Infrared Imager that JAXA supplied to Hera. Deimos is the small bright spot below the centre of a cooler Mars, because the airless, very dark moon absorbs sunlight and heats up while Mars is more reflective and moves heat around with its atmosphere. Hellas Basin is the cool purple region at the lower right, and a brightness temperature scale runs down the right-hand edge.

A near-infrared frame from HyperScout H, Hera's hyperspectral imager, which works in 25 visible and near-infrared bands to characterise surface materials. Mars is rendered pale blue and Deimos appears as a small dark ellipse in front of it, with Terra Sabaea at the top, the Huygens and 460 km Schiaparelli craters below it and Hellas Basin at the lower right.

A stereo pair of Deimos built from Hera's 12 March 2025 flyby frames by Sir Brian May of the Hera science team, published by ESA on 14 August 2026. A dashed white circle on the right-hand frame marks one of the ancient impact depressions lying under the moon's regolith blanket. Sabina Raducan says these buried features were not obvious by eye in the flat images and that the stereo rendering is what revealed them, supplying the last constraint on her Nature Astronomy reconstruction.
credit: S. D. Raducan, B. May/London Stereoscopic Company

caption: ESA's briefing graphic of 10 March 2025, published two days before the flyby. It gives Deimos a maximum diameter of 12.4 km and an orbit 20,068 km above the Martian surface, states that the trajectory brings Hera within 300 km of the moon while the three instruments will image it from a minimum of 1,000 km, labels the Asteroid Framing Camera, HyperScout H and the JAXA-supplied Thermal Infrared Imager on a drawing of the spacecraft, and sets Deimos beside the 780 m Didymos and the 151 m Dimorphos.

The two identical ESCAPADE orbiters, Blue and Gold, standing on dollies in a high bay of the Astrotech Space Operations Facility near Kennedy Space Center on 22 August 2024, where they were inspected and processed after delivery.
The second New Glenn lifting off from Space Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on 13 November 2025, the flight that carried the two ESCAPADE spacecraft away from Earth.
credit: U.S. Space Force photo by Samuel Becker

caption: Earth and the Moon as crescents, photographed on 3 July 2026 by one of the two ESCAPADE spacecraft from 584,600 km from Earth while it loitered in the Earth's neighbourhood waiting for the Mars window, with only about 8 per cent of each face sunlit.

The Idefix flight rover in its cruise configuration, published by ISAS with the caption 'IDEFIX Rover' alongside the 14 March 2024 announcement of the handover to JAXA at the Mitsubishi Electric Kamakura Works. The body is wrapped in gold and black thermal blanketing, two of its four wheels are folded flat against the flank facing the camera on their stowed hinged legs, and the top face carries the orange-red blanket over the folded solar panels studded with the open lattice crash pads that take the impact when the rover is dropped. It sits in a handling frame on protective sheeting, with a Centre National d'Etudes Spatiales label visible in the background.
credit: (c) ISAS/JAXA (rover built by CNES and DLR)

caption: Idefix in its stowed position on the MMX spacecraft at the Tanegashima Space Center, captioned by CNES as 'Insertion of an SD card inside Idefix®'. The rover is bolted to a spacecraft panel amid gold multi-layer insulation and black structure, red thermal blanket over its folded solar panels, lattice crash pads standing proud, wheels folded against its sides, while an engineer in cleanroom coveralls works at an opened flap on its upper face. Parts of the background are deliberately blurred in the frame CNES published.

A close-up of one folded wheel of the Idefix rover, photographed on 7 September 2023 in a cleanroom, showing the machined mesh-like wheel disc and the curved blades or grousers around its rim. The photographer's own caption describes the rover as folded and ready for flight before its transfer to Japan, and says the view focuses on a wheel with its special pads for moving on a soft Phobos surface.
credit: Ebottlaender, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

caption: Prototypix, the Earth prototype of Idefix, on the Phobos-analogue yard of DLR's Planetary Exploration Laboratory at Oberpfaffenhofen near Munich, during the four-day test campaign of late November 2025. The dark-bodied prototype carries DLR, CNES and JAXA markings, stands on four bright metal wheels with two of them lifted so the body is tilted back, and grooved wheel tracks run across the grey regolith simulant around it. Engineers watch from behind a rail at the edge of the yard. CNES's own caption reads 'Prototypix tests out the heliotropic sequence' and adds that the prototype is not hailing the Sun.

A figure from the rover team's own 2025 paper showing the autonomous uprighting sequence. The upper part is a schematic of the named body positions the rover moves through, Cruise, Parachutist, Flat, Inverse stowed, Stowed and Dragster, linked by coloured arrows with 'four legs at a time' on two of the transitions and a red branch marked 'If global Blockage counter is 8 or more'. The lower strip is four frames of the same manoeuvre rendered in a simulated environment, ending with the solar panels open. Every frame is either a diagram or a simulation.
credit: Ulamec, Michel, Murdoch et al., 'Science operations of IDEFIX, the MMX Phobos rover', Progress in Earth and Planetary Science 12, article 97, 23 October 2025, CC BY 4.0

caption: A frame from DLR's physics simulation of the rover driving on Phobos, captioned by DLR as 'The MMX Rover moving on Phobos (simulation)'. The vehicle is shown deployed, solar panels spread on both sides, wheels on the ground, with a shallow track behind it across a grey boulder-strewn surface under a black sky. The image carries a DLR Robotics and Mechatronics Center and Institute of System Dynamics and Control watermark at the top left and a simulation clock reading 'Time: 764.7200s' at the bottom left.
credit: DLR, Robotics and Mechatronics Center, Institute of System Dynamics and Control, CC BY 3.0 DE

caption: H3 flight 10 climbing into a dark sky on a long, bright exhaust plume, seen from below, with the core stage and its solid rocket boosters at the head of the flame and lit exhaust clouds along the bottom.

The whole H3 rocket rising off the pad at night, its orange core stage and white boosters lit by the flame, with the red and white lightning towers to the left, the umbilical tower to the right and exhaust clouds spreading along the ground.
The MMX spacecraft on a stand in a clean room, wrapped in gold thermal blanket, with a silver solar panel folded against its side, a dish antenna and dark struts folded above it.
H3 flight 10 rising on its exhaust plume above the launch pad at night, seen across the water, with the lit Vehicle Assembly Building at left and the ground cloud spreading to the right.

Close-up of the H3 flight 10 fairing with the MMX emblem large and sharp, the top of the core stage, and the red and white lightning towers and umbilical mast of the launch pad under a clear blue sky.

American and Japanese team members gathered around the gamma ray spectrometer part of MEGANE, the NASA-provided instrument that will measure the elemental composition of Phobos, during its development at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
The landing gear on a half-scale model of the MMX spacecraft displayed in the first floor atrium at the Japan Aerospace 2024 exhibition, Tokyo Big Sight, on 19 October 2024.

mission_name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
caption: A technician in a clean-room suit works at the base of the spacecraft NASA's caption calls Mariner I, standing inside the opened white panels of its protective enclosure at Kennedy Space Center in May 1971, before encapsulation, with the high-gain dish and the folded octagonal bus visible above him. It was designated Mariner 9 after the Atlas-Centaur launch of 30 May 1971.
credit: NASA Kennedy Space Center (KSC-71P-0366), via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
caption: The mating of the Viking 1 orbiter and lander in the Spacecraft Assembly and Encapsulation Facility at Kennedy Space Center in 1975. The lander is sealed out of sight inside its sterile bioshield, the white cap at the top and the wide foil-wrapped base beneath it, and the whole capsule is being lowered on a crane onto the orbiter bus, whose folded solar panels and red-tagged instrument boxes stand below.
credit: NASA (image 75-HC-111); scan by Cygni_18, via Wikimedia Commons

mission_name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
caption: Mars Global Surveyor in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 21 October 1996, its solar panels folded flat against the gold-blanketed bus, already mated to the solid propellant upper stage below it and standing in the lower half of its transfer canister while three workers in clean-room suits look on.

mission_name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
caption: A colour factory photograph of a 1F Phobos station in the assembly hall at the Lavochkin plant, the large thermally blanketed spherical propellant tanks of its Autonomous Propulsion Unit filling the frame above a lattice support frame and a mass of ground cabling, with red protective covers and tags still fitted and a technician on a platform at the right. The Lavochkin gallery carries no caption, date or serial number for the frame, only the alt text Проект, and the project page covers both flight articles, 1F No. 101 (Phobos 1) and 1F No. 102 (Phobos 2), so the picture cannot be pinned to either one.

mission_name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
caption: MAVEN on its transport pallet in the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center on 3 August 2013, its solar panels folded and instrument decks wrapped in silver blanketing, with a protective shroud suspended on a crane directly above it and a dozen engineers in blue clean-room suits standing around it, ahead of the November 2013 launch.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: HiRISE image of the Perseverance landing site in Jezero crater taken on 19 February 2021, one day after landing, with four objects labelled by the HiRISE team: the parachute and back shell at left, the crashed descent stage, the rover sitting in the pale blast pattern left by the hovering descent stage, and the heat shield at right.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: Enlargement from the HiRISE image of the Viking 1 landing site in western Chryse Planitia taken on 22 November 2006, showing the bright object HiRISE identifies as the likely back shell with the parachute attached to it. For everything other than the lander itself, HiRISE uses the words likely or candidate, and those identifications remain unconfirmed.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: Annotated cutout from the HiRISE image of the Spirit landing site in Gusev crater taken on 22 November 2006. Box a marks the parachute and the cone shaped back shell, box b the lander beside the crater the team named Sleepy Hollow, box c the damaged remnant of the heat shield, and box d Spirit itself, just southeast of the layered plateau the team named Home Plate.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: The first colour HiRISE view of the Opportunity landing site in Meridiani Planum, taken on 10 April 2017. HiRISE reports the lander as a darker centre amid reddish airbag material at the bottom of Eagle crater, the crumpled parachute still attached to the bluish back shell, and an arc of darker ground where the parachute has been blown about by the wind.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: Labelled HiRISE cutout of the InSight landing site in Elysium Planitia, imaged on 11 December 2018, marking the lander in the patch of dust disturbed by its thrusters, the back shell with its parachute, and the heat shield, which reads as a saturated bright spot. HiRISE interprets that brightness as a specular reflection and infers from it that the shield's dark outer face is turned downwards.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: HiRISE cutout of China's Tianwen-1 landing site in southern Utopia Planitia, imaged on 6 June 2021, three weeks after the 14 May landing. The lander sits inside a dark blast pattern with the Zhurong rover a short distance to the south, and a bright piece of discarded entry hardware appears at lower left; HiRISE identifies the parachute with its back shell and the heat shield separately in the same observation.

mission_name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
caption: Perseverance's back shell, left of centre, and its supersonic parachute at right, photographed from 8 m above the ground by the Ingenuity helicopter on its 26th flight on 19 April 2022, at the request of the Mars Sample Return team. The pair hit the ground at about 126 km/h after being jettisoned at 2.1 km altitude.

NPO Lavochkin's own computer rendering of the Boomerang spacecraft, published on its project page for КА «Бумеранг», ОКР «Экспедиция-М»: a transfer and landing platform on four legs with dished footpads, four solar wings, gold-blanketed spherical tanks and the return stack on top. The same page lists the launch as after 2030, the launcher as Angara-A5 and the mass as 5000 kg.

A Lavochkin exploded diagram of Phobos-Grunt, the 2011 spacecraft, labelled in Russian from the top down: спускаемый аппарат (the Earth entry capsule), возвращаемый аппарат (the return vehicle), перелетный модуль (the cruise and landing module), переходная ферма (the transfer truss), китайский микроспутник (the Chinese microsatellite Yinghuo-1), маршевая двигательная установка (the main propulsion unit) and сбрасываемый блок баков (the jettisonable tank block). Every part of it is drawn.

A Phobos-Grunt vehicle standing on its landing legs and dished footpads in an assembly hall at the Lavochkin plant, large spherical propellant tanks and instrument boxes exposed, a stowed panel above and handling equipment around it. The Lavochkin gallery publishes the frame with no caption and no date, so whether this is the flight article or a test article is not established.

Dr V. Narayanan seated at ISRO Headquarters in Bengaluru on 15 January 2025, the day ISRO announced he had begun functioning there, beneath the State Emblem of India and the wall lettering 'Government of India, Department of Space, ISRO Headquarters' in English and Hindi. The frame carries ISRO's own on-screen caption naming him Secretary, Department of Space and Chairman, ISRO.
credit: Department of Space / Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)

caption: An LVM3 lifting off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, on the LVM3-M5 mission carrying the CMS-03 communications satellite on 2 November 2025. The vehicle is caught at the instant of lift-off with its two solid strap-on boosters burning, still level with the swing arms of the service structure and flanked by both lightning towers, and the SDSC SHAR sign is visible at the base.
