A frame of 王小军 (Wang Xiaojun), president of the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology, delivering his plenary report by video link, seated at a table in front of the CALT sign reading 中国运载火箭技术研究院 and China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology (CALT), with the subtitle "The Space Transportation System of Human Mars Exploration" across the bottom.
credit: 中国航天报 (China Space News), via Sina Technology

caption: A display model of the Long March 9 super heavy-lift launch vehicle standing in an exhibition hall at Airshow China in Zhuhai in November 2022, marked CHN, 中国航天 and LONG MARCH 9, with a smaller crewed launch vehicle model beside it and visitors for scale.

SpaceX's own render of the 2016 Interplanetary Transport System, published by the company on 27 September 2016 with the caption 'Interplanetary Spaceship, arriving Mars'. The nose and upper hull of the vehicle fill the lower left of the frame, its thermal tiles picked out as dark dashes along the flank, with Mars beyond it in the upper right of the frame, lit from the right and its terminator crossing the lower left of the disc.

SpaceX's render of orbital propellant transfer, published on 27 September 2016 with the caption 'An Interplanetary tanker (left) transferring propellant to an Interplanetary Spaceship (right), in Earth orbit'. The two vehicles are mated tail to tail high above a sunlit ocean and cloud, the thin blue limb of the atmosphere and black space at the right of the frame.

SpaceX's own concept art, captioned by the company 'Concept art of sending Dragon to Mars', showing a Dragon capsule marked SPACEX and DRAGON hovering just above a dusty Martian surface with four landing legs extended and its SuperDraco thrusters firing, dust and grit blown outward across the frame.

A photograph of the full Starship stack climbing away from Starbase in south Texas on flight test 11, dated 13 October 2025, seen across water and a low bank of rock and grass, the vehicle already well above a wide bank of grey and dust-coloured exhaust cloud with the engine plume beneath it.
credit: Shujianyang, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

caption: A row of desk-sized Starship design models on a sideboard at the SpaceX Design Center, photographed on 22 June 2023, each on a small labelled stand, one card reading 'PROTOTYPE, PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH'. Above them hangs a backlit SpaceX marketing render of passengers eating together in a lit cabin. The photographer's note says he also saw full-scale mock-ups of the bathroom and sleep quarters for the missions to Mars.
credit: Steve Jurvetson, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

caption: BIG's aerial visualisation of Mars Science City as it would sit in the desert outside Dubai, five geodesic domes clustered on a green plot beside a looping access road, with a highway at the left and a hazy sunrise behind.
BIG's visualisation of the same domes transposed onto Mars, lit from within and full of palms, with a rover in the foreground on a rocky red plain under a dusty sky.

The prime and alternate crew of HERA Campaign 7 Mission 4 standing in dark flight suits outside the Human Exploration Research Analog habitat at NASA's Johnson Space Center, holding the mission patch lettered Wilder, Hundley, Magas, Alsuwaidi, Snyder and Wilson, with a UAE flag on the patch and on one crew member's sleeve.

Officials and students applauding beside the newly unveiled dark stone sign of the Korea AeroSpace Administration at Sacheon, the stone carrying the government emblem, the words 대한민국우주항공청 and the inscribed date 2024. 5. 27, photographed at the opening ceremony on 30 May 2024.
credit: 경상남도 우주항공산업과 (Aerospace Industry Division, South Gyeongsang Province), via Wikimedia Commons, KOGL Type 1

caption: The Mars Chopper concept in a design software rendering on a plain white background: six rotor hubs, each carrying six black carbon-fibre blades, held out on a trussed carbon frame, with a small gold solar panel above every hub, a transparent central payload box holding a green circuit board, and slender legs ending in ball feet. NASA's caption states that Chopper would be about the size of an SUV and that it remains in early conceptual and design stages, a collaboration between JPL, NASA Ames and AeroVironment Inc.

The six-rotor Mars Science Helicopter shown against a plain grey studio gradient: a flat hexagonal body with a violet solar array on its upper face, six arms carrying four-bladed rotors, and a soft shadow beneath. NASA's page is headed Model of Proposed Mars Science Helicopter and says a model of the concept is shown in this photo, without saying whether the model is physical or built in software; the image itself reads as a computer rendering. NASA states the vehicle would carry 2 to 5 kg of payload and remains in early conceptual and design stages.

A photograph at the open door of the 25-Foot Space Simulator at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the black ribbed chamber wall on the left and the bright high bay beyond. Engineer Jaakko Karras, in a white cleanroom smock and gloves, reaches up to the motor can under the hub of a three-bladed next-generation rotor slung from an aluminium test rig, its plain black carbon-fibre blades held horizontally and copper instrumentation tape running along the beams. A second rotor stands behind it with its disc vertical, carrying two blades marked in a black and white checkerboard pattern. NASA's caption names Karras and dates the frame to November 2025, describing it as an inspection of a next-generation rotor blade before supersonic speed testing.

A chamber camera frame stamped 2023-09-15 18:13:13, showing the dual rotor test rig standing on the floor of JPL's 25-Foot Space Simulator: a bare aluminium truss carrying a rotor on a canted arm, blades marked with a checkerboard pattern, a white cloth backdrop hung behind them and the black ribbed wall of the vacuum chamber all around. NASA states the carbon-fibre blades reached Mach 0.95 at the tips during this three-week campaign.

An artist's concept of the Mars Life Explorer standing on rocky ground under a pale orange sky: a lander in the Phoenix and InSight mould, with two circular fan-fold solar arrays spread either side, instrument boxes on the deck, and a tall vertical drill mast reaching down to the surface beside the leg. The Planetary Society captions it as the Mars Life Explorer operating on the surface with its drill deployed. Nothing has been built.

A HiRISE excerpt from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing a small fresh impact crater in the northern mid-latitudes, a bright white patch of excavated ice at its centre surrounded by a dark blast scar on rippled orange ground, with a 100 metre scale bar. NASA's record states that the impact exposed bright ice that had been hidden just beneath the surface at this location.

The Subsurface Water Ice Mapping map, a grey shaded-relief Mars base with the Tharsis volcanoes and Valles Marineris across the lower half and a broad blue wash covering the northern plains, marking where NASA missions have detected subsurface water ice. Triangles are past and present landed missions, circles are ice-exposing impact craters. NASA's record states that the project mapped from the equator to 60 degrees north, hunting ice in the mid-latitudes: far enough toward the pole for water ice to be plentiful, but close enough to the equator to avoid the coldest temperatures on Mars.

A NASA artist's concept of the SkyFall manoeuvre, seen from below, with three small helicopters flying away from the aeroshell while it still hangs beneath its inflated parachute in the Martian atmosphere.

NASA image PIA26760, an artist's concept of the three SkyFall helicopters working over Martian ground, with green cones drawn beneath their antennas to represent ground-penetrating radar sounding and red beams to represent near-infrared imaging of the regolith.

The banner still from AV's Skyfall reveal, showing a helicopter flying clear of the capsule as it descends under its parachute, with the words ARTIST'S CONCEPT printed in the top right corner by the company.

mission_name: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
caption: An Impulse Space render of the Mars Cruise Vehicle, a small spacecraft with two black solar panels, flying beside the released entry capsule and its blunt heat shield above a mostly sunlit Mars, with the night side falling away at the left limb.

mission_name: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
caption: An Impulse Space render of the proposed Mars lander, a four-legged vehicle descending on two engines through a dust-coloured Martian sky with the ground faintly visible below.

mission_name: Commercial Mars Payload Services and Mars Future Missions
caption: A NASA mission profile diagram titled Space Reactor-1 Freedom Flight Path, showing Earth orbit, Mars orbit and the SR-1 trajectory as coloured curves around the Sun, with seven numbered events from launch in late 2028 through reactor startup at 30 days, a first Mars flyby at 300 days, release of the SkyFall capsule at 600 days and helicopter deployment at 660 days.

mission_name: Commercial Mars Payload Services and Mars Future Missions
caption: A frame from AeroVironment's Skyfall visualisation showing a ring of coaxial rotor helicopters clamped to a truss beneath a descending aeroshell over the Martian surface, the moment before the helicopters are released to fly themselves down.

mission_name: Commercial Mars Payload Services and Mars Future Missions
caption: NASA's artist's concept of the Space Reactor-1 Freedom spacecraft passing Mars, showing a silver central body with two large purple and white solar arrays, grey radiator panels, a long boom carrying the reactor away from the bus, and the blue plumes of its Hall thrusters.

ESA's artist's impression of LightShip, released 21 January 2025, showing the electric propulsion tug over Mars with two large solar wings and three blue ion plumes, and a smaller passenger spacecraft that has just separated flying alongside it.
A wider, portrait framing of the same ESA artist's impression, captioned by ESA simply as Artist's impression of LightShip, with the tug and its released passenger small against the limb of Mars.

An ESA infographic from its Ten things you did not know about Mars series, panel 2, showing a rover on Mars relaying through an orbiter to a ground antenna on Earth, and stating that the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter relays around 60 per cent of NASA's Mars surface data and that signals take between about 4 and 24 minutes each way.

A NASA montage of artist's illustrations of the five orbiters that made up the Mars Relay Network when it was published in February 2021, captioned by NASA clockwise from top left as Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, MAVEN, Mars Odyssey, and ESA's Mars Express and Trace Gas Orbiter, arranged around a globe of Mars.
Rocket Lab's rendering of its proposed Mars telecommunications orbiter above Mars, a bus carrying a large white high-gain dish, a smaller steerable antenna and a single flat solar wing.
Blue Origin's rendering of a Blue Ring derived Mars communications spacecraft in deep space, with a mesh high-gain dish on a boom, two long solar wings and Mars small in the background.

mission_name: Aeolus and the Relativity Mars orbiter
caption: A Relativity Space computer render of the company's proposed Mars orbiter, a compact boxy bus carrying two long multi-panel solar wings, coasting in front of a fully lit Mars.

mission_name: Aeolus and the Relativity Mars orbiter
caption: A photograph of NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman announcing the public-private partnership at Relativity Space on 17 June 2026, addressing a large seated and standing crowd on the factory floor with a United States flag and a long Relativity-branded rocket stage lying horizontally behind him.

Perseverance's Mastcam-Z panorama of the finished sample depot at Three Forks in Jezero crater, taken on 31 January 2023 and stitched from 368 frames. The titanium sample tubes laid out on the ground are each about 18 cm long and 2 cm across.

NASA and ESA concept illustration from April 2022 of the Mars Sample Return campaign, showing Perseverance at far left, the Sample Retrieval Lander at right carrying the Mars Ascent Vehicle, and the sample recovery helicopters.
A development motor based on the second stage solid rocket motor design for the Mars Ascent Vehicle firing on a test stand at Northrop Grumman's facility in Elkton, Maryland, on 29 March 2023.
NASA artist's concept published in June 2019 depicting astronauts and human habitats on the surface of Mars. Nothing in the picture exists; no crewed Mars mission has been funded or approved.

The near side of the Moon seen through a window of the Orion spacecraft on 5 April 2026, Flight Day 5 of Artemis II and the night before the crew's lunar flyby. NASA's caption describes commander Reid Wiseman looking out at the Moon before going to sleep; the agency credits the photograph to NASA rather than to a named crew member.

NASA's artist's concept of Space Reactor-1 Freedom passing Mars, showing the two large solar wings of the Gateway Power and Propulsion Element, a long truss boom carrying the reactor and its radiators, and the blue plume of an electric thruster firing.

NASA's Space Reactor-1 Freedom Flight Path graphic, plotting the SR-1 trajectory against the orbits of Earth and Mars and numbering seven events: launch in late 2028, solar array deployment at one day, reactor startup at 30 days, a first Mars flyby at 300 days, release of the SkyFall capsule at 600 days, and a second Mars flyby and atmospheric entry at 660 days.

A cleanroom photograph of Gateway's Power and Propulsion Element undergoing battery installation at Lanteris Space Systems in Palo Alto, California, showing the flight bus on its handling fixture with multi-layer insulation, orange cabling and a painted United States flag on its side.
credit: Lanteris Space Systems, via NASA (nasa_id jsc2026e005278)

caption: The ExoMars rover under construction in the bio-burden controlled cleanroom at Airbus Defence and Space in Stevenage, photographed in February 2019, the month the rover was named after Rosalind Franklin.
The mission's 74 kg, 35 m diameter main parachute, made mostly of nylon and Kevlar, wrapped in a ring shaped bag and about to be sterilised in a dry heat oven, photographed by ESA in April 2026.

One of the three metre ramps that will carry the Rosalind Franklin rover down off its landing platform, photographed fully deployed with its guide rails inside a thermal vacuum chamber after a release test at about minus 70 C. Published by ESA on 21 July 2026.

Rendering issued by China News Service in December 2025 of the Tianwen-3 orbiter and return module combination, labelled in the original Chinese caption as a simulation image (天问三号探测器轨返组合体模拟图). China News Service issued the rendering rather than a photograph of hardware.
